papers.abstract: Recent work by Anthropic on Mechanistic interpretability claims to understand and control Large Language Models by extracting human-interpretable features from their neural activation patterns using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). If successful, this approach offers one of the most promising routes for human oversight in AI safety. We conduct an initial stress-test of these claims by replicating their main results with open-source SAEs for Llama 3.1. While we successfully reproduce basic feature extraction and steering capabilities, our investigation suggests that major caution is warranted regarding the generalizability of these claims. We find that feature steering exhibits substantial fragility, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context. We observe non-standard activation behavior and demonstrate the difficulty to distinguish thematically similar features from one another. While SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases, current methods often fall short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications. This suggests a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of what mechanistic interpretability has achieved and highlights fundamental challenges for AI safety that remain unresolved.

papers.title: The Birth of Knowledge: Emergent Features across Time, Space, and Scale in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper studies the emergence of interpretable categorical features within large language models (LLMs), analyzing their behavior across training checkpoints (time), transformer layers (space), and varying model sizes (scale). Using sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, we identify when and where specific semantic concepts emerge within neural activations. Results indicate clear temporal and scale-specific thresholds for feature emergence across multiple domains. Notably, spatial analysis reveals unexpected semantic reactivation, with early-layer features re-emerging at later layers, challenging standard assumptions about representational dynamics in transformer models.

papers.title: Causal Intervention Framework for Variational Auto Encoder Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can causal interventions be used to understand the internal mechanisms of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a causal intervention framework for mechanistic interpretability of VAEs, enabling identification of circuit motifs and quantification of interpretability metrics.
papers.conclusion: The causal intervention framework enables detailed understanding of VAE internal mechanisms, with insights into circuit specialization and disentanglement, paving the way for more transparent generative models.
papers.key_findings:
VAEs develop specialized circuit motifs for processing different semantic factors.
FactorVAE achieves higher disentanglement scores and effect strengths compared to standard VAE and β-VAE.
Modularity alone doesn't guarantee disentanglement; causal effect strength is equally important.
Early encoder layers contain polysemantic units, while latent space shows more monosemantic units in FactorVAE.
Causal mediation analysis reveals layer-specific and dimension-specific information flow patterns.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other generative models like diffusion models and GANs
Use insights to design more transparent and controllable generative models
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Mechanistic interpretability of deep learning models has emerged as a crucial research direction for understanding the functioning of neural networks. While significant progress has been made in interpreting discriminative models like transformers, understanding generative models such as Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) remains challenging. This paper introduces a comprehensive causal intervention framework for mechanistic interpretability of VAEs. We develop techniques to identify and analyze "circuit motifs" in VAEs, examining how semantic factors are encoded, processed, and disentangled through the network layers. Our approach uses targeted interventions at different levels: input manipulations, latent space perturbations, activation patching, and causal mediation analysis. We apply our framework to both synthetic datasets with known causal relationships and standard disentanglement benchmarks. Results show that our interventions can successfully isolate functional circuits, map computational graphs to causal graphs of semantic factors, and distinguish between polysemantic and monosemantic units. Furthermore, we introduce metrics for causal effect strength, intervention specificity, and circuit modularity that quantify the interpretability of VAE components. Experimental results demonstrate clear differences between VAE variants, with FactorVAE achieving higher disentanglement scores (0.084) and effect strengths (mean 4.59) compared to standard VAE (0.064, 3.99) and \(\beta\)-VAE (0.051, 3.43). Our framework advances the mechanistic understanding of generative models and provides tools for more transparent and controllable VAE architectures.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: DiffusionPID: Interpreting Diffusion via Partial Information Decomposition
papers.research_question: How do individual tokens and their interactions in a text prompt shape the image generated by a text-to-image diffusion model? The paper investigates what diffusion models learn, how they represent visual-semantic relationships, and why they sometimes fail to generalize.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DiffusionPID, a method based on partial information decomposition (PID) to interpret text-to-image diffusion models by decomposing the input prompt into elementary components and analyzing uniqueness, redundancy, and synergy at both image and pixel levels.
papers.conclusion: DiffusionPID allows for a fine-grained understanding of the decision-making process in diffusion models, helping to identify shortcomings and reasons for failures. This understanding can be used to make diffusion models better aligned with human conceptual understanding and to counter their limitations and biases.
papers.key_findings:
DiffusionPID can reveal gender and ethnic biases in diffusion models by showing higher redundancy between stereotypical occupations and specific genders/ethnicities.
The method characterizes word ambiguity and similarity from the model's perspective, showing high synergy for homonyms with correct modifiers and high redundancy for synonyms.
DiffusionPID enables prompt intervention by identifying redundant words whose removal minimally affects the generated image.
The uniqueness maps can localize the most representative features of a concept, such as the bristles of a toothbrush.
The method provides fine-grained insights into model failures, such as confusing co-hyponyms due to high redundancy, leading to fused or missing objects in generations.
papers.limitation:
The method currently computes PID only for two phrases from the prompt, though it can be extended to more variables.
The approach requires access to the diffusion model, making it difficult to apply to closed-source models.
future_direction: Extending PID to more than two input variables.
Computing PID on other, non-diffusion-based models.
Exploring alternative methods of computing PID for closed-source models.
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have made significant progress in generating naturalistic images from textual inputs, and demonstrate the capacity to learn and represent complex visual-semantic relationships. While these diffusion models have achieved remarkable success, the underlying mechanisms driving their performance are not yet fully accounted for, with many unanswered questions surrounding what they learn, how they represent visual-semantic relationships, and why they sometimes fail to generalize. Our work presents Diffusion Partial Information Decomposition (DiffusionPID), a novel technique that applies information-theoretic principles to decompose the input text prompt into its elementary components, enabling a detailed examination of how individual tokens and their interactions shape the generated image. We introduce a formal approach to analyze the uniqueness, redundancy, and synergy terms by applying PID to the denoising model at both the image and pixel level. This approach enables us to characterize how individual tokens and their interactions affect the model output. We first present a fine-grained analysis of characteristics utilized by the model to uniquely localize specific concepts, we then apply our approach in bias analysis and show it can recover gender and ethnicity biases. Finally, we use our method to visually characterize word ambiguity and similarity from the model's perspective and illustrate the efficacy of our method for prompt intervention. Our results show that PID is a potent tool for evaluating and diagnosing text-to-image diffusion models.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of LoRA-Adapted Language Models for Nuclear Reactor Safety Applications
papers.research_question: How does LoRA adaptation alter neuron activation patterns in an LLM for a nuclear reactor safety domain, and what is the causal role of these altered neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a methodology for tracing domain expertise in a LoRA-adapted LLM to a sparse set of neurons and demonstrates that the model's expertise is an emergent property of a neural circuit, providing a pathway for nuclear-grade AI assurance.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates a replicable methodology for moving beyond treating LLMs as opaque black boxes towards a mechanistic understanding of their function, offering a pathway to achieve nuclear-grade AI assurance by identifying, monitoring, and causally testing knowledge-bearing neural circuits.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA fine-tuning on a BWR dataset induced systematic changes in the activation patterns of a small set of neurons in the final MLP layer.
Silencing the entire group of six key neurons collectively caused a statistically significant degradation in BLEU score, while silencing most individual neurons did not, supporting a circuit-based view of knowledge encoding.
Qualitative analysis revealed distinct functional roles for key neurons, such as encoding core technical concepts (#1066, #1086), suppressing generalist language (#941), and representing procedural logic (#176).
The adapted model produced more concise and precise answers than the base model, as measured by a decrease in average answer length and an increase in BLEU score.
The findings suggest that verifying the integrity of distributed neural circuits, rather than individual components, is crucial for safety assurance in nuclear applications.
papers.limitation: The reliance on the BLEU score, while justified for measuring output precision, does not verify factual accuracy.
future_direction: Development of domain-specific evaluation metrics that can automatically verify technical correctness against a trusted knowledge base.
Extending the methodology to other critical nuclear systems, including Pressurized Water Reactors (PWRs) and advanced reactor designs.
Validating the approach across different model architectures, model scales, and technical documentation corpora.
papers.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into safety-critical domains, such as nuclear engineering, necessitates a deep understanding of their internal reasoning processes. This paper presents a novel methodology for interpreting how an LLM encodes and utilizes domain-specific knowledge, using a Boiling Water Reactor system as a case study. We adapted a general-purpose LLM (Gemma-3-1b-it) to the nuclear domain using a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique known as Low-Rank Adaptation. By comparing the neuron activation patterns of the base model to those of the fine-tuned model, we identified a sparse set of neurons whose behavior was significantly altered during the adaptation process. To probe the causal role of these specialized neurons, we employed a neuron silencing technique. Our results demonstrate that while silencing most of these specialized neurons individually did not produce a statistically significant effect, deactivating the entire group collectively led to a statistically significant degradation in task performance. Qualitative analysis further revealed that silencing these neurons impaired the model's ability to generate detailed, contextually accurate technical information. This paper provides a concrete methodology for enhancing the transparency of an opaque black-box model, allowing domain expertise to be traced to verifiable neural circuits. This offers a pathway towards achieving nuclear-grade artificial intelligence (AI) assurance, addressing the verification and validation challenges mandated by nuclear regulatory frameworks (e.g., 10 CFR 50 Appendix B), which have limited AI deployment in safety-critical nuclear operations.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning? Are they essential for pattern matching in ICL?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that induction heads are essential for few-shot in-context learning, as their ablation leads to significant performance drops in both abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks.
papers.conclusion: The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, and induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying ICL.
papers.key_findings:
Ablation of 1% of induction heads leads to substantial ICL performance decreases (up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks).
For NLP tasks, ablation of induction heads reduces the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot performance close to zero-shot.
Attention knockout experiments show that blocking the induction pattern causes performance drops comparable to full head ablations, confirming the specific role of the prefix matching and copying mechanism.
The effects are consistent across two models (Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B).
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of prefix matching and copying for pattern matching.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for induction heads without mechanistic verification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks, not verified across NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL).However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking.This paper explores the role of induction heads in a fewshot ICL setting.We analyse two state-of-theart models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks.Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random.For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts.We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present finegrained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: APP: Accelerated Path Patching with Task-Specific Pruning
papers.research_question: Can pruning be used for circuit discovery, and how can we accelerate path patching by reducing the search space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid method that uses Contrastive-FLAP pruning to reduce the search space for circuit discovery, achieving significant speedups while recovering minimal circuits with performance comparable to standard path patching.
papers.conclusion: APP provides a scalable preprocessing step for circuit discovery, making mechanistic interpretability more efficient and practical for large models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning alone cannot recover minimal circuits; circuits found by pruning are larger than those found by path patching.
Contrastive-FLAP, a novel pruning method, better preserves task-specific attention heads compared to vanilla FLAP.
APP reduces the search space for circuit discovery by an average of 56%, leading to speedups of 59.63%-93.27% compared to standard path patching.
Circuits discovered by APP have substantial overlap and similar performance to those found by standard path patching.
APP enables circuit discovery to scale to larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) by reducing computational costs.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter search is limited by computational cost, especially for large models.
Trade-off between circuit size and performance requires researcher discretion.
APP focuses on attention heads and does not include MLP components, which may be important for some tasks.
The true positive rate of hybrid FLAP caps the ability to recover all heads in the circuit.
future_direction: Extending APP to other circuit discovery algorithms like ACDC.
Incorporating MLP components into the automated path patching method.
Studying whether circuits discovered in GPT-2 small translate to larger models.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery is a key step in many mechanistic interpretability pipelines. Current methods, such as Path Patching, are computationally expensive and have limited in-depth circuit analysis for smaller models. In this study, we propose Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid approach leveraging our novel contrastive attention head pruning method to drastically reduce the search space of circuit discovery methods. Our Contrastive-FLAP pruning algorithm uses techniques from causal mediation analysis to assign higher pruning scores to task-specific attention heads, leading to higher performing sparse models compared to traditional pruning techniques. Although Contrastive-FLAP is successful at preserving task-specific heads that existing pruning algorithms remove at low sparsity ratios, the circuits found by Contrastive-FLAP alone are too large to satisfy the minimality constraint required in circuit analysis. APP first applies Contrastive-FLAP to reduce the search space on required for circuit discovery algorithms by, on average, 56\%. Next, APP, applies traditional Path Patching on the remaining attention heads, leading to a speed up of 59.63\%-93.27\% compared to Path Patching applied to the dense model. Despite the substantial computational saving that APP provides, circuits obtained from APP exhibit substantial overlap and similar performance to previously established Path Patching circuits

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: Studying Cross-cluster Modularity in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of training neural networks to be modular using a clusterability loss on interpretability, such as task specialization and circuit size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a clusterability measure and loss function to train neural networks to be modular. Shows that modular models do not exhibit more task specialization but have smaller circuits, aiding interpretability.
papers.conclusion: A simple regularizer can split neural network layers into non-interacting modules, but these modules do not yield expected interpretability benefits like task specialization. However, modularity improves circuit size and search space without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models are not modular; clusters are highly enmeshed.
Training with clusterability loss effectively increases modularity in models.
Modular models do not show increased task specialization compared to non-modular models.
Modular models have smaller effective circuits, reducing circuit size.
Theoretical analysis indicates modularity simplifies function spaces and reduces the number of features.
papers.limitation: The modularity metric does not lead to clear interpretability benefits such as task specialization.
future_direction: Investigate alternative regularizers for interpretability benefits.
Build an automated subtask detection mechanism.
papers.abstract: An approach to improve neural network interpretability is via clusterability, i.e., splitting a model into disjoint clusters that can be studied independently. We define a measure for clusterability and show that pre-trained models form highly enmeshed clusters via spectral graph clustering. We thus train models to be more modular using a "clusterability loss" function that encourages the formation of non-interacting clusters. We then investigate the emerging properties of these highly clustered models. We find our trained clustered models do not exhibit more task specialization, but do form smaller circuits. We investigate CNNs trained on MNIST and CIFAR, small transformers trained on modular addition, and GPT-2 and Pythia on the Wiki dataset, and Gemma on a Chemistry dataset. This investigation shows what to expect from clustered models.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability, and how can we define and demarcate mechanistic interpretability as a scientific practice?
papers.core_contribution: The paper defines mechanistic interpretability as the practice of producing model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable explanations of neural networks, and argues that the Principle of Explanatory Optimism is a necessary precondition for its success.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability is a valuable scientific practice for understanding neural networks, grounded in the Explanatory View and dependent on the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, and provides a framework for defining and pursuing faithful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal mechanisms (ur-explanations), not just its input-output behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability is formally defined as seeking explanations that are model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable.
Mechanistic interpretability has inherent limits due to the value-ladenness and theory-ladenness of explanations, and its focus on model-level explanations excludes system-level complexities.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism states that the algorithmic structure learned by generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, and without this assumption, mechanistic interpretability is intractable.
papers.limitation:
Explanations in mechanistic interpretability are value-laden, as the choice of precision and metrics depends on the interpreter's goals and values.
Explanations are theory-laden, as interpretability methods rely on theoretical commitments (e.g., sparse autoencoders assume sparsity and linearity).
Mechanistic interpretability focuses on model-level explanations, but AI systems involve additional components beyond the model, limiting the scope of MI for understanding system behavior.
future_direction: Increased focus on criteria that make explanations accessible to diverse humans, involving human-computer interaction and social sciences.
Development of a new field focusing on system-level explanations, building on mechanistic interpretability.
Collaboration between philosophy, computational complexity, and machine learning to investigate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural net- works through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability re- search is a principled approach to understanding models be- cause neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI’s inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Patterning: The Dual of Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the dual problem to interpretability? The paper introduces patterning as the dual: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data leads to it.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces patterning as the dual of interpretability, using susceptibilities to derive data interventions that steer internal structure formation in neural networks, demonstrated in small language models and a synthetic task.
papers.conclusion: Patterning provides a principled approach to steering generalization by inverting the susceptibility relationship, with potential applications to AI alignment and control of internal structure.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting training data along the second principal susceptibility direction can accelerate or delay the formation of the induction circuit.
In the parentheses balancing task, patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution.
Susceptibility-guided interventions produce predictable changes in internal structures.
papers.limitation:
Experiments use small models (3M parameters) and simple tasks.
Susceptibility estimation is computationally expensive.
Focus on one-off interventions made at the start of training, not online control.
Theoretical framework assumes infinitesimal perturbations, while practical interventions are finite; understanding when the linear approximation breaks down is important.
Connection between observables and downstream behavior (e.g., safety properties) requires further study.
future_direction: Develop online control (adjusting data distribution dynamically during training).
Scale to larger models and more efficient methods.
Study the connection to safety properties and AI alignment applications.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how neural networks generalize beyond their training data by reverse-engineering their internal structures. We introduce patterning as the dual problem: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data produces it. Our approach is based on susceptibilities, which measure how posterior expectation values of observables respond to infinitesimal shifts in the data distribution. Inverting this linear response relationship yields the data intervention that steers the model toward a target internal configuration. We demonstrate patterning in a small language model, showing that re-weighting training data along principal susceptibility directions can accelerate or delay the formation of structure, such as the induction circuit. In a synthetic parentheses balancing task where multiple algorithms achieve perfect training accuracy, we show that patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution. These results establish that the same mathematical framework used to read internal structure can be inverted to write it.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability -- The Strange Science Part I.i
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability? How can we define mechanistic interpretability and what are its inherent limits?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a philosophical framework for mechanistic interpretability, including the Explanatory View Hypothesis, a definition of mechanistic interpretability as producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations, and the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that if the Principle of Explanatory Optimism holds, interpretability could enable humans to understand machine knowledge, making it a crucial scientific endeavor for the future of human understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory Faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal ur-explanations, and is well-defined under the Explanatory View.
Mechanistic Interpretability is defined as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks.
Mechanistic Interpretability has inherent limits, such as theory-ladenness and the potential for high explanatory complexity that may make models incomprehensible to humans.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism, which states that the algorithmic structure of generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability may be limited by the theory-ladenness of observations, where the interpreter's prior theories influence what they can discover.
There is a risk that the explanatory complexity of models might be too high for humans to understand, which would make mechanistic interpretability intractable.
future_direction: Formalize the conjectures of Strong and Weak Explanatory Optimism, including defining explanatory complexity classes and explanatory universality.
Prove the formalized conjectures to assess the truth value of the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural networks through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability research is a principled approach to understanding models because neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI's inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: CLIP is All You Need for Human-like Semantic Representations in Stable Diffusion
papers.research_question: Does Stable Diffusion's internal representations during text-to-image generation contain human-like semantic information, and is this due to CLIP or the diffusion process?
papers.core_contribution: The semantic understanding in Stable Diffusion comes from the pretrained CLIP model, not the reverse diffusion process, which instead acts as a visual decoder of CLIP's representations.
papers.conclusion: CLIP is primarily responsible for the human-like semantic representations in Stable Diffusion, and the diffusion process serves as a visual decoder. Non-spatial attributes are more accurately decoded than spatial ones.
papers.key_findings:
Most human attribute ratings can be predicted from Stable Diffusion's latent representations with accuracy significantly below chance.
The semantic representation is most human-like at the output of CLIP, and the reverse diffusion process degrades this alignment.
Non-spatial attributes are more accurately decoded than spatial attributes across all model components.
CLIP can disentangle attributes that humans entangle, while the diffusion process tends to entangle attributes.
Attributes become more difficult to disambiguate from one another during the inverse diffusion process.
papers.limitation: The study uses a dataset of text prompts and human attribute ratings, but lacks a corresponding image dataset with attribute labels, limiting the analysis to text-based prompts.
future_direction: Applying the probing technique to other generative models (e.g., GANs, other diffusion models) to compare human alignment.
Creating an image dataset labeled with attribute ratings to generalize results to generated images.
Investigating how well language-only and vision-language models align with human perception.
papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion achieve state-of-the-art results on text-to-image generation tasks. However, the extent to which these models have a semantic understanding of the images they generate is not well understood. In this work, we investigate whether the internal representations used by these models during text-to-image generation contain semantic information that is meaningful to humans. To do so, we perform probing on Stable Diffusion with simple regression layers that predict semantic attributes for objects and evaluate these predictions against human annotations. Surprisingly, we find that this success can actually be attributed to the text encoding occurring in CLIP rather than the reverse diffusion process. We demonstrate that groups of specific semantic attributes have markedly different decoding accuracy than the average, and are thus represented to different degrees. Finally, we show that attributes become more difficult to disambiguate from one another during the inverse diffusion process, further demonstrating the strongest semantic representation of object attributes in CLIP. We conclude that the separately trained CLIP vision-language model is what determines the human-like semantic representation, and that the diffusion process instead takes the role of a visual decoder.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: FeatInv: Spatially resolved mapping from feature space to input space using conditional diffusion models
papers.research_question: How can we learn a high-fidelity, probabilistic mapping from spatially resolved feature maps to input space to improve feature space understanding in computer vision models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes FeatInv, a method that uses a conditional diffusion model (ControlNet) to learn a high-fidelity, probabilistic mapping from spatially resolved feature maps to input space, enabling improved visualization and understanding of feature spaces in computer vision models.
papers.conclusion: FeatInv provides an effective probabilistic mapping from feature space to input space using a conditional diffusion model, enabling accurate and robust reconstruction across different model architectures and offering valuable applications for model interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
FeatInv can reconstruct high-fidelity natural images from feature maps of various models (ResNet50, ConvNeXt, SwinV2).
Using unpooled (spatially resolved) feature maps yields better reconstruction quality (higher cosine similarity and top5 match) and sample quality (lower FID) than using pooled feature maps.
The method is robust and generalizes across models (cross-model evaluation) and to out-of-distribution data (BAID dataset).
FeatInv enables applications such as FeatInv-Viz for visualizing concept steering in input space and investigating the composite nature of feature space via linear interpolations and spatial compositions.
Conditioning on earlier feature layers provides more detailed and accurate reconstructions, and the faithfulness of reconstruction extends beyond the specific layer used for conditioning.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on the domain of natural images.
Requires a pretrained diffusion model, which might not be readily available in all application contexts.
Every model and layer choice requires training a dedicated FeatInv model, representing a computational hurdle.
Application scenarios rely on modifications of the feature space, and there is a need for measures to detect input samples (feature maps) that are outside the scope of the model.
future_direction: Extend the approach to other domains, such as medical imaging.
Investigate finetuning to alleviate the need for training a model per layer.
Introduce measures to detect input samples (feature maps) that are outside the scope of the model.
papers.abstract: Internal representations are crucial for understanding deep neural networks, such as their properties and reasoning patterns, but remain difficult to interpret. While mapping from feature space to input space aids in interpreting the former, existing approaches often rely on crude approximations. We propose using a conditional diffusion model - a pretrained high-fidelity diffusion model conditioned on spatially resolved feature maps - to learn such a mapping in a probabilistic manner. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach across various pretrained image classifiers from CNNs to ViTs, showing excellent reconstruction capabilities. Through qualitative comparisons and robustness analysis, we validate our method and showcase possible applications, such as the visualization of concept steering in input space or investigations of the composite nature of the feature space. This approach has broad potential for improving feature space understanding in computer vision models.

papers.title: Compact Proofs of Model Performance via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to derive compact formal guarantees on model performance? Does more compact proof require and provide more mechanistic understanding, and does more faithful understanding lead to tighter bounds?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can be used to generate compact formal proofs of model performance, and shows that more compact proofs require more mechanistic understanding and that more faithful understanding leads to tighter bounds.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability can be used to generate compact proofs of model performance, but compounding structureless errors pose a challenge that future work must address.
papers.key_findings:
Shorter proofs seem to require and provide more mechanistic understanding.
More faithful mechanistic understanding leads to tighter performance bounds.
Compounding structureless errors is a key challenge for using mechanistic interpretability to generate compact proofs on model performance.
papers.limitation:
Compounding structureless errors pose a challenge for generating compact proofs.
The approach is demonstrated only on a simple toy setting (Max-of-K).
future_direction: Addressing the challenge of compounding structureless errors in generating compact proofs.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and models.
papers.abstract: We propose using mechanistic interpretability -- techniques for reverse engineering model weights into human-interpretable algorithms -- to derive and compactly prove formal guarantees on model performance. We prototype this approach by formally proving accuracy lower bounds for a small transformer trained on Max-of-K, validating proof transferability across 151 random seeds and four values of K. We create 102 different computer-assisted proof strategies and assess their length and tightness of bound on each of our models. Using quantitative metrics, we find that shorter proofs seem to require and provide more mechanistic understanding. Moreover, we find that more faithful mechanistic understanding leads to tighter performance bounds. We confirm these connections by qualitatively examining a subset of our proofs. Finally, we identify compounding structureless errors as a key challenge for using mechanistic interpretability to generate compact proofs on model performance.

papers.title: On the Mechanistic Interpretability of Neural Networks for Causality in Bio-statistics
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability techniques be transposed to bio-statistics, and how effective are they?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability tools can be leveraged to probe and validate internal representations learned by neural networks for causal inference, discover and visualize computational pathways for confounders and treatments, and compare learned mechanisms across model types.
papers.abstract: Interpretable insights from predictive models remain critical in bio-statistics, particularly when assessing causality, where classical statistical and machine learning methods often provide inherent clarity. While Neural Networks (NNs) offer powerful capabilities for modeling complex biological data, their traditional "black-box" nature presents challenges for validation and trust in high-stakes health applications. Recent advances in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aim to decipher the internal computations learned by these networks. This work investigates the application of MI techniques to NNs within the context of causal inference for bio-statistics. We demonstrate that MI tools can be leveraged to: (1) probe and validate the internal representations learned by NNs, such as those estimating nuisance functions in frameworks like Targeted Minimum Loss-based Estimation (TMLE); (2) discover and visualize the distinct computational pathways employed by the network to process different types of inputs, potentially revealing how confounders and treatments are handled; and (3) provide methodologies for comparing the learned mechanisms and extracted insights across statistical, machine learning, and NN models, fostering a deeper understanding of their respective strengths and weaknesses for causal bio-statistical analysis.

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a single learning problem (modular addition), and scaling the techniques to more complex models and real-world tasks requires significant additional work.
future_direction: How to find, classify, and interpret unfamiliar algorithms in a systematic way.
How to disentangle multiple, parallel algorithm implementations in the presence of ensembling.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.

papers.title: Multi-Granular Node Pruning for Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we perform circuit discovery at multiple granularities (down to neurons) in a scalable way, overcoming the limitations of existing edge-pruning methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a node-level pruning framework for circuit discovery that operates at multiple granularities (from blocks to neurons) in a single optimization step, achieving higher efficiency and finer granularity than existing edge-pruning methods.
papers.conclusion: The node pruning approach is efficient and effective for circuit discovery, achieving substantial reductions in circuit size and number of retained attention heads, and suggests future work combining edge and node pruning for even more minimal circuits.
papers.key_findings:
The structure of discovered circuits depends on the task; for example, all MLP blocks are essential for the IOI task, while for the GT task, most MLPs can be removed.
Different component granularities exhibit varying susceptibility to compression; for instance, the outputs of MLP1 (Keys) can be sparsified to a much greater extent than those of MLP2 (Values).
The method identifies circuits that are smaller in nodes than those discovered by prior methods while maintaining task performance.
The method reveals that many neurons within components deemed important by coarse methods are actually irrelevant.
The method has a significantly lower memory footprint (5-10x) compared to baselines, as it does not require storing intermediate activations.
papers.limitation: The framework discovers node-level circuits but does not explicitly recover the interaction structure between nodes, such as which active nodes exchange information and the directionality of those interactions.
future_direction: Combining edge and node pruning in a hierarchical fashion
Developing a hybrid node and edge procedure to infer interaction structure
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery aims to identify minimal subnetworks that are responsible for specific behaviors in large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches primarily rely on iterative edge pruning, which is computationally expensive and limited to coarse-grained units such as attention heads or MLP blocks, overlooking finer structures like individual neurons. We propose a node-level pruning framework for circuit discovery that addresses both scalability and granularity limitations. Our method introduces learnable masks across multiple levels of granularity, from entire blocks to individual neurons, within a unified optimization objective. Granularity-specific sparsity penalties guide the pruning process, allowing a comprehensive compression in a single fine-tuning run. Empirically, our approach identifies circuits that are smaller in nodes than those discovered by prior methods; moreover, we demonstrate that many neurons deemed important by coarse methods are actually irrelevant, while still maintaining task performance. Furthermore, our method has a significantly lower memory footprint, 5-10x, as it does not require keeping intermediate activations in the memory to work.

papers.title: Efficient Representations are Controllable Representations
papers.research_question: What is the most brute-force way to install interpretable, controllable features into a model’s activations? Can a model's efficiency pressure be exploited to induce interpretable, controllable representations?
papers.core_contribution: By finetuning an LLM with a simple auxiliary loss to write binary feature classifications into a small set of residual stream dimensions, the model reorganizes to depend on these flags, making them genuine internal features that can be used to steer generation at inference time. This works due to the model's efficiency pressure under capacity constraints.
papers.conclusion: The residual stream is writable, and a model's own efficiency pressure can be exploited to induce interpretable and controllable representations. This inverts the usual controllability problem by providing signals that the model will naturally consolidate around.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns to write correct feature flags to the designated 'fenced' dimensions after training.
The model learns to depend on these flags during generation, as shown by overwriting experiments that causally steer generation.
The model erodes its own alternative representations of the fenced features, consolidating feature information into the fenced dimensions.
The efficiency pressure (representational cost) leads the model to consolidate around the reliably supplied feature signals.
The method incurs a negligible perplexity cost when fencing a small number of dimensions, but the cost grows as more dimensions are fenced.
papers.limitation:
Early layers (k < 5) struggle to produce clean flags, consistent with the view that early layers have not yet derived the relevant features.
At the current level of training, the model has begun to erode previous representations but some residual information persists in the remaining dimensions.
papers.abstract: What is the most brute-force way to install interpretable, controllable features into a model's activations? Controlling how LLMs internally represent concepts typically requires sophisticated methods to first identify, then intervene on the model's existing feature geometry. We bypass all of this. We finetune an LLM with a simple auxiliary loss, training 16 of its 3072 residual stream dimensions to be inert interpretability flags that simply indicate what concepts are required for generation. The model reorganizes around them anyway, learning to rely on these flags during actual generation tasks. As a result, these inert flags become genuine internal features: interpretable control switches that allow us to steer generation at inference time. Why does this work? When a feature is reliably supplied at a fixed location, gradient descent gradually eliminates redundant encodings elsewhere, and the model erodes its own alternative representations. A model's efficiency pressure is a lever - exploitable to induce interpretable, controllable representations.

papers.title: Analyze Feature Flow to Enhance Interpretation and Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do features discovered by sparse autoencoders evolve across consecutive layers of large language models, and how can this understanding be used for interpretability and model steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a data-free cosine similarity method to map Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features across transformer layers, creating flow graphs that reveal feature evolution and enable precise model steering through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed cross-layer feature mapping framework provides granular interpretability of feature evolution in LLMs and offers a new, transparent method for steering model behavior through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Cosine similarity between SAE decoder weights effectively identifies feature relationships across layers, validated against activation correlations.
Feature formation follows distinct patterns: early layers show high entropy and feature birth, middle layers stabilize, and later layers primarily propagate existing features.
Deactivating predecessor features identified by the top-1 cosine match is causally effective, outperforming random selection.
Multi-layer steering using flow graphs is more effective and less sensitive to hyperparameters than single-layer interventions.
Flow graphs provide mechanistic insights, revealing how semantic meaning (e.g., 'particle physics') evolves and transforms across the model's computational pathway.
papers.limitation: The current steering procedure operates locally on hidden states and may not fully redirect the model's computational trajectory to a different 'minima' for truly efficient deactivation or activation.
future_direction: Further research on flow graphs as a unit of study for model interpretability.
Extending the steering experiments and flow graph analysis to other model architectures like Llama Scope.
Investigating the method's applicability and performance across a wider range of models and SAE training configurations.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new approach to systematically map features discovered by sparse autoencoder across consecutive layers of large language models, extending earlier work that examined inter-layer feature links. By using a data-free cosine similarity technique, we trace how specific features persist, transform, or first appear at each stage. This method yields granular flow graphs of feature evolution, enabling fine-grained interpretability and mechanistic insights into model computations. Crucially, we demonstrate how these cross-layer feature maps facilitate direct steering of model behavior by amplifying or suppressing chosen features, achieving targeted thematic control in text generation. Together, our findings highlight the utility of a causal, cross-layer interpretability framework that not only clarifies how features develop through forward passes but also provides new means for transparent manipulation of large language models.

papers.title: Improving Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks in Medical Diagnosis by Investigating the Individual Units
papers.research_question: How can attribution techniques like LRP and RAP improve the interpretability of DNNs in medical diagnosis by visualizing significant factors and revealing inconsistencies between human and DNN intentions?
papers.core_contribution: Attribution methods like LRP and RAP can effectively localize lesions in chest X-rays without bounding box supervision and reveal that DNNs may learn based on normal lung features rather than disease lesions, highlighting the need for interpretability in medical diagnosis.
papers.conclusion: Attribution techniques such as LRP and RAP offer efficient ways to interpret DNN decisions in medical diagnosis by localizing lesions and uncovering potential inconsistencies, underscoring the necessity of explainability for reliable adoption.
papers.key_findings:
LRP and RAP achieve higher IOU scores than CAM for localizing lesions in chest X-ray images, indicating better visualization accuracy.
Attribution methods provide detailed pixel-wise explanations compared to CAM's broad visualizations from resized feature maps.
DNNs trained for pneumonia classification may focus on normal lung features rather than pneumonia lesions, showing inconsistency with human intentions.
CheXNet, pretrained for multiple diseases, provides clear visual explanations aligned with lesion areas, unlike models trained only on pneumonia data.
The study emphasizes the importance of explainability to ensure DNNs' decision criteria align with clinical expectations.
papers.abstract: As interpretability has been pointed out as the obstacle to the adoption of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), there is an increasing interest in solving a transparency issue to guarantee the impressive performance. In this paper, we demonstrate the efficiency of recent attribution techniques to explain the diagnostic decision by visualizing the significant factors in the input image. By utilizing the characteristics of objectness that DNNs have learned, fully decomposing the network prediction visualizes clear localization of target lesion. To verify our work, we conduct our experiments on Chest X-ray diagnosis with publicly accessible datasets. As an intuitive assessment metric for explanations, we report the performance of intersection of Union between visual explanation and bounding box of lesions. Experiment results show that recently proposed attribution methods visualize the more accurate localization for the diagnostic decision compared to the traditionally used CAM. Furthermore, we analyze the inconsistency of intentions between humans and DNNs, which is easily obscured by high performance. By visualizing the relevant factors, it is possible to confirm that the criterion for decision is in line with the learning strategy. Our analysis of unmasking machine intelligence represents the necessity of explainability in the medical diagnostic decision.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Working Mechanism of Text-to-Image Diffusion Model
papers.research_question: How does the text-to-image diffusion model work, specifically the role of text prompts and the denoising process?
papers.core_contribution: The denoising process in T2I diffusion models first reconstructs shape (low-frequency) and then details (high-frequency), and the text prompt (especially the [EOS] token) primarily influences the early shape reconstruction stage, enabling accelerated sampling by removing text guidance later.
papers.conclusion: The working mechanism of T2I diffusion models involves a two-stage process: shape reconstruction followed by detail filling, with text prompt influence concentrated in the first stage, which can be leveraged for acceleration.
papers.key_findings:
The denoising process recovers low-frequency signals (shape) first and high-frequency signals (details) later.
The special token [EOS] dominates the influence of the text prompt on the generated image, especially for shape.
The text prompt information is conveyed primarily in the early denoising stage (shape reconstruction), and later stages rely more on the image itself.
Removing text guidance in later denoising steps can accelerate sampling by 25%+ without significant quality loss.
papers.abstract: Recently, the strong latent Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DPM) has been applied to high-quality Text-to-Image (T2I) generation (e.g., Stable Diffusion), by injecting the encoded target text prompt into the gradually denoised diffusion image generator. Despite the success of DPM in practice, the mechanism behind it remains to be explored. To fill this blank, we begin by examining the intermediate statuses during the gradual denoising generation process in DPM. The empirical observations indicate, the shape of image is reconstructed after the first few denoising steps, and then the image is filled with details (e.g., texture). The phenomenon is because the low-frequency signal (shape relevant) of the noisy image is not corrupted until the final stage in the forward process (initial stage of generation) of adding noise in DPM. Inspired by the observations, we proceed to explore the influence of each token in the text prompt during the two stages. After a series of experiments of T2I generations conditioned on a set of text prompts. We conclude that in the earlier generation stage, the image is mostly decided by the special token [\texttt{EOS}] in the text prompt, and the information in the text prompt is already conveyed in this stage. After that, the diffusion model completes the details of generated images by information from themselves. Finally, we propose to apply this observation to accelerate the process of T2I generation by properly removing text guidance, which finally accelerates the sampling up to 25\%+.

papers.title: Evaluating Brain-Inspired Modular Training in Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does modular training (BIMT) affect the efficiency and quality of automated circuit discovery? How does modularity impact computational efficiency (training memory, time, inference)?
papers.core_contribution: Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT) significantly improves the efficiency and quality of automated circuit discovery, producing sparser circuits with lower logit differences and faster discovery times, though with increased training memory and time.
papers.conclusion: BIMT is an innovative and practical approach to neural network interpretability, enabling more efficient and effective circuit discovery, which is critical for analyzing large-scale models.
papers.key_findings:
BIMT achieves lower logit difference (1.2737 for circle detection) compared to other training regimes, indicating better circuit quality.
BIMT discovers circuits faster (93.76 seconds for circle detection) than other models.
BIMT produces sparser circuits (0.9859 sparsity for circle detection) which are easier to interpret.
BIMT requires more memory during training due to the swap operation, and has longer training times.
BIMT has slightly higher inference times compared to L1-only model (65.77 vs 64.65 seconds for 500000 images).
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to the MNIST dataset and MLP architecture, which may not generalize to other tasks and models.
Modular training may cause neurons to become polysemantic due to superposition, which could hinder interpretability.
future_direction: Test BIMT on transformer networks.
Investigate the effect of modularity on superposition.
Use attribution patching instead of activation patching for larger networks.
Evaluate BIMT on other tasks beyond digit classification.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have experienced a rapid rise in AI, changing a wide range of applications with their advanced capabilities. As these models become increasingly integral to decision-making, the need for thorough interpretability has never been more critical. Mechanistic Interpretability offers a pathway to this understanding by identifying and analyzing specific sub-networks or 'circuits' within these complex systems. A crucial aspect of this approach is Automated Circuit Discovery, which facilitates the study of large models like GPT4 or LLAMA in a feasible manner. In this context, our research evaluates a recent method, Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT), designed to enhance the interpretability of neural networks. We demonstrate how BIMT significantly improves the efficiency and quality of Automated Circuit Discovery, overcoming the limitations of manual methods. Our comparative analysis further reveals that BIMT outperforms existing models in terms of circuit quality, discovery time, and sparsity. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive computational analysis of BIMT, including aspects such as training duration, memory allocation requirements, and inference speed.
