This study advances the larger objective of creating trustworthy and transparent AI systems in addition to demonstrating how well BIMT works to make neural networks easier to understand.

papers.title: Preserving Bilinear Weight Spectra with a Signed and Shrunk Quadratic Activation Function
papers.research_question: Can we design an activation function for Gated Linear Units (GLUs) that enables weight-based interpretability (via eigen-features) without sacrificing performance and data efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Signed Quadratic Shrink (SQS), an activation function for GLUs that preserves the weight structure properties of bilinear MLPs (enabling interpretability via eigen-decomposition) while achieving performance competitive with state-of-the-art activation functions.
papers.conclusion: Signed Quadratic Shrink (SQS) is an activation function that enables the development of interpretable features via weight spectra while providing performance on par with, and in some scenarios better than, standard activation functions.
papers.key_findings:
SQS-GLU learns interpretable features, as shown by eigenvector decomposition of its weight matrices, similar to bilinear MLPs.
SQS achieves performance (loss, accuracy, perplexity) competitive with or better than ReLU, GELU, and SwiGLU on MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and Tiny Stories.
SQS converges faster and achieves lower loss than ReLU-GLUs and Bilinear MLPs on the image classification tasks.
The eigenvectors from SQS-GLU show high cosine similarity with those from Bilinear MLPs, indicating preserved interpretability.
SQS maintains computational efficiency comparable to other activation functions when implemented with specific hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of machine learning models is critical for ensuring their reliability and robustness. Whilst many techniques in mechanistic interpretability focus on activation driven analyses, being able to derive meaningful features directly from the weights of a neural network would provide greater guarantees and more computational efficiency. Existing techniques for analyzing model features through weights suffer from drawbacks such as reduced performance and data inefficiency. In this paper, we introduce Signed Quadratic Shrink (SQS), an activation function designed to allow Gated Linear Units (GLUs) to learn interpretable features without these drawbacks. Our experimental results show that SQS achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art activation functions whilst enabling weight-based interpretability

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the key open problems in mechanistic interpretability methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges that need to be addressed to achieve the field's goals?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes and outlines key open problems in mechanistic interpretability, covering methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges to guide future research.
papers.conclusion: The review outlines critical open problems in mechanistic interpretability that must be addressed to achieve scientific and engineering goals, emphasizing the need for methodological improvements and socio-technical integration.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability methods, such as sparse dictionary learning, suffer from practical and conceptual limitations like high reconstruction errors and unclear theoretical foundations.
Applying interpretability to AI safety requires robust methods for monitoring internal states and controlling behavior, but current techniques are insufficient.
Socio-technical challenges include integrating interpretability into AI governance and addressing philosophical questions about the field's goals.
future_direction: Developing better decomposition methods like sparse dictionary learning with lower reconstruction errors.
Creating validation frameworks for interpretability hypotheses.
Applying interpretability to AI safety monitoring and control.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the computational mechanisms underlying neural networks' capabilities in order to accomplish concrete scientific and engineering goals. Progress in this field thus promises to provide greater assurance over AI system behavior and shed light on exciting scientific questions about the nature of intelligence. Despite recent progress toward these goals, there are many open problems in the field that require solutions before many scientific and practical benefits can be realized: Our methods require both conceptual and practical improvements to reveal deeper insights; we must figure out how best to apply our methods in pursuit of specific goals; and the field must grapple with socio-technical challenges that influence and are influenced by our work. This forward-facing review discusses the current frontier of mechanistic interpretability and the open problems that the field may benefit from prioritizing.

papers.title: The Computational Complexity of Circuit Discovery for Inner Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the computational complexity of circuit discovery queries for inner interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a complexity analysis of circuit discovery queries, showing that many are intractable (NP-hard, Σp2-hard, etc.), but also identifies tractable relaxations such as quasi-minimal circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that circuit discovery for inner interpretability is computationally challenging, but identifies tractable relaxations and provides a framework for understanding the complexity of interpretability queries.
papers.key_findings:
Many circuit discovery queries (e.g., sufficient circuit, circuit ablation) are NP-hard or Σp2-hard.
Some queries remain fixed-parameter intractable (W[1]-hard) even when parameterizing by model depth or other features.
Some queries are inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes.
There is a formal separation between local and global query complexity, which helps explain interpretability illusions.
Quasi-minimal circuit queries are tractable (PTIME) and retain useful affordances for description and control.
future_direction: Empirical and formal characterization of learned weights to inform average-case analyses.
Exploring more parameters for fixed-parameter tractability in circuit discovery queries.
Designing queries that rely on mid-level abstractions to bridge circuits and human-intelligible algorithms.
papers.abstract: Many proposed applications of neural networks in machine learning, cognitive/brain science, and society hinge on the feasibility of inner interpretability via circuit discovery. This calls for empirical and theoretical explorations of viable algorithmic options. Despite advances in the design and testing of heuristics, there are concerns about their scalability and faithfulness at a time when we lack understanding of the complexity properties of the problems they are deployed to solve. To address this, we study circuit discovery with classical and parameterized computational complexity theory: (1) we describe a conceptual scaffolding to reason about circuit finding queries in terms of affordances for description, explanation, prediction and control; (2) we formalize a comprehensive set of queries for mechanistic explanation, and propose a formal framework for their analysis; (3) we use it to settle the complexity of many query variants and relaxations of practical interest on multi-layer perceptrons. Our findings reveal a challenging complexity landscape. Many queries are intractable, remain fixed-parameter intractable relative to model/circuit features, and inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes. To navigate this landscape, we prove there exist transformations to tackle some of these hard problems with better-understood heuristics, and prove the tractability or fixed-parameter tractability of more modest queries which retain useful affordances. This framework allows us to understand the scope and limits of interpretability queries, explore viable options, and compare their resource demands on existing and future architectures.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine\n Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops unsupervised methods (based on correlations between models) for discovering important neurons in Neural Machine Translation models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates how to control translations by modifying their activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and that many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Moreover, modifying the activations of individual neurons allows controlling the translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Unsupervised correlation methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) can rank neurons by importance, with top-ranked neurons having a larger impact on translation quality when erased.
Many top-ranked neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as position in sentence, parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Modifying the activations of individual neurons (e.g., tense neurons) allows for controlling translation output (e.g., changing verb tense) with varying degrees of success.
Different ranking methods highlight different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find information distributed across tokens.
The work indicates that not all linguistic information in NMT models is fully distributed; some properties are captured by individual neurons.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional seq2seq).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Apply the methods to other tasks beyond machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing
substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such
information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to
individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important
neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models
learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision.
We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered
neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena.
Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by
modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Localized Concept Erasure in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models via High-Level Representation Misdirection
papers.research_question: How to effectively erase target concepts in text-to-image diffusion models by updating only early layers of the text encoder to misdirect high-level representations, thereby preserving generative utility?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes HiRM, a concept erasure method that decouples update location (early layers) and erasure target (high-level representations) in the text encoder, enabling precise concept removal with minimal impact on unrelated concepts.
papers.conclusion: HiRM is an effective method for concept erasure that balances erasure performance and utility preservation, and is transferable across models.
papers.key_findings:
HiRM achieves strong performance on UnlearnCanvas benchmark for style and object erasure.
HiRM is robust to adversarial and NSFW prompts.
HiRM preserves generative utility and has low training cost.
HiRM transfers to state-of-the-art architectures (Flux) and LoRA-augmented models without additional training.
HiRM shows synergistic effects when combined with denoiser-based concept erasing methods.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have seen rapid and widespread adoption. However, their powerful generative capabilities raise concerns about potential misuse for synthesizing harmful, private, or copyrighted content. To mitigate such risks, concept erasure techniques have emerged as a promising solution. Prior works have primarily focused on fine-tuning the denoising component (e.g., the U-Net backbone). However, recent causal tracing studies suggest that visual attribute information is localized in the early self-attention layers of the text encoder, indicating a potential alternative for concept erasing. Building on this insight, we conduct preliminary experiments and find that directly fine-tuning early layers can suppress target concepts but often degrades the generation quality of non-target concepts. To overcome this limitation, we propose High-Level Representation Misdirection (HiRM), which misdirects high-level semantic representations of target concepts in the text encoder toward designated vectors such as random directions or semantically defined directions (e.g., supercategories), while updating only early layers that contain causal states of visual attributes. Our decoupling strategy enables precise concept removal with minimal impact on unrelated concepts, as demonstrated by strong results on UnlearnCanvas and NSFW benchmarks across diverse targets (e.g., objects, styles, nudity). HiRM also preserves generative utility at low training cost, transfers to state-of-the-art architectures such as Flux without additional training, and shows synergistic effects with denoiser-based concept erasing methods.

papers.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we perform fine-grained circuit analysis through MLP sublayers in transformers, given the polysemanticity of neurons? The paper proposes transcoders as a solution to enable input-invariant circuit analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces transcoders, a method for approximating MLP sublayers with sparse, interpretable features, enabling input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders are an effective tool for decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits, enabling scalable and interpretable circuit analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders are as interpretable as SAEs and perform similarly or better in terms of sparsity and faithfulness.
Transcoders enable circuit analysis that factorizes into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, allowing for general claims about model behavior.
Blind case studies demonstrate that transcoders can reverse-engineer features without looking at activating examples.
Analysis of the GPT2-small greater-than circuit reveals new insights, such as the role of the MLP0 layer.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders may not capture all nuances of the original MLP, as seen in the 'caught' feature example where the transcoder did not accurately model the difference between 'was caught' and 'caught the ball'.
Blind case studies had some failures, indicating that circuit analysis with transcoders is not always perfect.
future_direction: Scaling transcoders to larger models.
Applying transcoders to more tasks and models.
papers.abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.

papers.title: Explaining Visual Models by Causal Attribution
papers.research_question: How can we compute the effects of interventions on latent factors to explain the predictions of deep learning image classifiers using causal counterfactuals?
papers.core_contribution: A novel explanation methodology for visual models based on causal counterfactuals, using Distributional Causal Graphs to sample from intervened models and estimate intervention effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal counterfactuals are essential for reliable explanations of visual models, and the DCG approach can account for causal dependencies, but a proper counterfactual image generator is still needed for real-world image data.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Distributional Causal Graph (DCG) can model causal relationships between latent factors and allow sampling from intervened distributions.
Current conditional image generators (CausalGAN, Fader Networks, AttGAN) have limitations for counterfactual image generation, as they do not properly consider causal structure and have issues with reconstruction and adversarial training.
The method can identify which latent factors are responsible for a classifier's prediction error, as demonstrated in a synthetic experiment with the 3D Shapes dataset.
papers.limitation:
Current conditional image generators (CausalGAN, Fader Networks, AttGAN) are insufficient for counterfactual image generation due to causal blindness and sensitivity to loss weights.
The method is only tested on a synthetic dataset because of the lack of a suitable image generator for real images.
future_direction: Developing a counterfactual image generator that meets the desiderata: causal generator, reconstruction loss only on non-causal factors, and adversarial training.
papers.abstract: Model explanations based on pure observational data cannot compute the effects of features reliably, due to their inability to estimate how each factor alteration could affect the rest. We argue that explanations should be based on the causal model of the data and the derived intervened causal models, that represent the data distribution subject to interventions. With these models, we can compute counterfactuals, new samples that will inform us how the model reacts to feature changes on our input. We propose a novel explanation methodology based on Causal Counterfactuals and identify the limitations of current Image Generative Models in their application to counterfactual creation.

papers.title: Interpreting and Improving Adversarial Robustness of Deep Neural Networks With Neuron Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How does neuron sensitivity relate to adversarial robustness, and can stabilizing sensitive neurons improve model robustness against adversarial examples?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces neuron sensitivity as a measure for adversarial robustness and proposes the Sensitive Neuron Stabilizing (SNS) method to improve robustness by stabilizing the behaviors of sensitive neurons.
papers.conclusion: Neuron sensitivity is closely related to adversarial robustness, and stabilizing sensitive neurons can effectively improve model robustness against adversarial examples.
papers.key_findings:
Sensitive neurons (those with high behavior variation between benign and adversarial examples) make the most non-trivial contributions to model misclassification in adversarial settings.
State-of-the-art adversarial training methods improve model robustness by reducing neuron sensitivities.
Stabilizing sensitive neurons via the proposed SNS method effectively improves adversarial robustness across various datasets and attack methods.
There exists a trade-off between robustness and accuracy, and sensitive neurons are responsible for both clean accuracy and robustness.
Adversarial attacks exploit sensitive neurons differently at different layers, with bottom layers focusing on common low-level features and top layers on class-specific features.
papers.limitation:
Uses the same coefficient λ to combine sensitivities in different layers, which might not be optimal due to heterogeneous behaviors of different layers.
The layer selection method is a naive top-k procedure, which may not adapt well to various model architectures.
future_direction: Use adaptive coefficients that consider heterogeneous behaviors of different layers to make full use of each intermediate layer.
Develop a better layer selection strategy that adapts to various model architectures.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial examples where inputs with imperceptible perturbations mislead DNNs to incorrect results. Despite the potential risk they bring, adversarial examples are also valuable for providing insights into the weakness and blind-spots of DNNs. Thus, the interpretability of a DNN in the adversarial setting aims to explain the rationale behind its decision-making process and makes deeper understanding which results in better practical applications. To address this issue, we try to explain adversarial robustness for deep models from a new perspective of neuron sensitivity which is measured by neuron behavior variation intensity against benign and adversarial examples. In this paper, we first draw the close connection between adversarial robustness and neuron sensitivities, as sensitive neurons make the most non-trivial contributions to model predictions in the adversarial setting. Based on that, we further propose to improve adversarial robustness by stabilizing the behaviors of sensitive neurons. Moreover, we demonstrate that state-of-the-art adversarial training methods improve model robustness by reducing neuron sensitivities, which in turn confirms the strong connections between adversarial robustness and neuron sensitivity. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate that our algorithm effectively achieves excellent results. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study adversarial robustness using neuron sensitivities.

papers.title: Efficiently Democratizing Medical LLMs for 50 Languages via a Mixture of Language Family Experts
papers.research_question: How to efficiently adapt medical Large Language Models to many languages, especially low-resource ones, by analyzing internal information flow and using language family experts?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an efficient method to scale medical LLMs to 50 languages via language family experts and a Post-MoE architecture, based on the discovery of the 'Spread Out in the End' information flow mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Apollo-MoE method efficiently democratizes medical LLMs to 50 languages, demonstrating strong generalization and scalability.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered the 'Spread Out in the End' mechanism in multilingual MoE models: early layers concentrate cross-lingual information flow, later layers exhibit language-specific divergence.
Proposed Post-MoE architecture (MoE only in later layers) improves generalization to low-resource languages.
Introduced language family experts, enabling scaling to many languages without adding parameters.
Hybrid-k routing (language-specific experts with cross-lingual routing) outperforms Top-k and Language-Specific routing.
papers.abstract: Adapting medical Large Language Models to local languages can reduce barriers to accessing healthcare services, but data scarcity remains a significant challenge, particularly for low-resource languages. To address this, we first construct a high-quality medical dataset and conduct analysis to ensure its quality. In order to leverage the generalization capability of multilingual LLMs to efficiently scale to more resource-constrained languages, we explore the internal information flow of LLMs from a multilingual perspective using Mixture of Experts (MoE) modularity. Technically, we propose a novel MoE routing method that employs language-specific experts and cross-lingual routing. Inspired by circuit theory, our routing analysis revealed a Spread Out in the End information flow mechanism: while earlier layers concentrate cross-lingual information flow, the later layers exhibit language-specific divergence. This insight directly led to the development of the Post-MoE architecture, which applies sparse routing only in the later layers while maintaining dense others. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach enhances the generalization of multilingual models to other languages while preserving interpretability. Finally, to efficiently scale the model to 50 languages, we introduce the concept of language family experts, drawing on linguistic priors, which enables scaling the number of languages without adding additional parameters.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: Enhancing Automated Interpretability with Output-Centric Feature Descriptions
papers.research_question: How can we generate faithful feature descriptions for LLMs by considering both the inputs that activate a feature and its causal effect on model outputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes efficient, output-centric methods (VocabProj and TokenChange) for automatically generating feature descriptions in LLMs, and demonstrates that combining these with input-centric methods yields the most faithful descriptions across both input and output evaluations.
papers.conclusion: Output-centric methods provide efficient and effective ways to generate feature descriptions that capture causal effects, and their combination with input-centric methods yields more faithful and complete descriptions, enhancing automated interpretability pipelines.
papers.key_findings:
Output-centric feature descriptions (VocabProj, TokenChange) better capture the causal effect of a feature on model outputs than the prevalent input-centric method (MaxAct).
Combining input- and output-centric methods (ensembles) leads to the best performance on both input- and output-based evaluations of description faithfulness.
Output-centric methods are computationally efficient, requiring only a few inference passes, and can serve as a cheap alternative to MaxAct in some cases.
Output-centric descriptions can be used to find inputs that activate 'dead' features for which no activating inputs were previously identified.
Performance varies by layer and feature type, with output-based performance being lower for MLP features compared to residual stream features.
papers.abstract: Automated interpretability pipelines generate natural language descriptions for the concepts represented by features in large language models (LLMs), such as plants or the first word in a sentence. These descriptions are derived using inputs that activate the feature, which may be a dimension or a direction in the model's representation space. However, identifying activating inputs is costly, and the mechanistic role of a feature in model behavior is determined both by how inputs cause a feature to activate and by how feature activation affects outputs. Using steering evaluations, we reveal that current pipelines provide descriptions that fail to capture the causal effect of the feature on outputs. To fix this, we propose efficient, output-centric methods for automatically generating feature descriptions. These methods use the tokens weighted higher after feature stimulation or the highest weight tokens after applying the vocabulary "unembedding" head directly to the feature. Our output-centric descriptions better capture the causal effect of a feature on model outputs than input-centric descriptions, but combining the two leads to the best performance on both input and output evaluations. Lastly, we show that output-centric descriptions can be used to find inputs that activate features previously thought to be "dead".

papers.title: Scale Alone Does not Improve Mechanistic Interpretability in Vision Models
papers.research_question: Does scaling model and dataset size improve the mechanistic interpretability of vision models at the level of individual units?
papers.core_contribution: Scaling model and dataset size does not improve the mechanistic interpretability of vision models at the level of individual units, and latest-generation models may even be less interpretable than older ones.
papers.conclusion: Scale alone does not improve mechanistic interpretability in vision models; explicit design for interpretability is needed, and the released dataset can facilitate research on automated interpretability measures.
papers.key_findings:
No practically relevant differences in interpretability across nine vision models of varying scales, indicating that scaling does not improve interpretability.
Feature visualizations are less helpful than natural exemplars for explaining unit activations across all models, including adversarially robust models.
Interpretability does not increase with model classification performance or human-likeness, and may even decrease for feature visualizations as accuracy increases.
For models pre-trained on large datasets (Clip ResNet and Clip ViT), later layers are more interpretable, suggesting a shift in interpretability across layers.
Interpretability drops sharply when the task difficulty increases slightly, indicating that human understanding of unit behavior is limited.
papers.limitation:
The study only employed two widely-used explanation methods (feature visualizations and natural exemplars), which may not capture all aspects of interpretability.
Feature visualizations for ViT models were not evaluated due to methodological challenges, limiting the comparison for transformer architectures.
future_direction: Designing models explicitly for interpretability rather than relying on scale.
Developing automated interpretability measures using the released dataset to avoid costly human evaluations.
Further research on interpretability methods beyond feature visualizations and natural exemplars.
papers.abstract: In light of the recent widespread adoption of AI systems, understanding the internal information processing of neural networks has become increasingly critical. Most recently, machine vision has seen remarkable progress by scaling neural networks to unprecedented levels in dataset and model size. We here ask whether this extraordinary increase in scale also positively impacts the field of mechanistic interpretability. In other words, has our understanding of the inner workings of scaled neural networks improved as well? We use a psychophysical paradigm to quantify one form of mechanistic interpretability for a diverse suite of nine models and find no scaling effect for interpretability - neither for model nor dataset size. Specifically, none of the investigated state-of-the-art models are easier to interpret than the GoogLeNet model from almost a decade ago. Latest-generation vision models appear even less interpretable than older architectures, hinting at a regression rather than improvement, with modern models sacrificing interpretability for accuracy. These results highlight the need for models explicitly designed to be mechanistically interpretable and the need for more helpful interpretability methods to increase our understanding of networks at an atomic level. We release a dataset containing more than 130'000 human responses from our psychophysical evaluation of 767 units across nine models. This dataset facilitates research on automated instead of human-based interpretability evaluations, which can ultimately be leveraged to directly optimize the mechanistic interpretability of models.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models Reveals the Hierarchical Nature of Data
papers.research_question: How do diffusion models capture the hierarchical and compositional structure of data? Specifically, how do they operate at different hierarchical levels of features over different time scales?
papers.core_contribution: Diffusion models exhibit a phase transition in reconstructing high-level features (like class) at a threshold time, while low-level features evolve smoothly, revealing the hierarchical nature of data.
papers.conclusion: Diffusion models act at different hierarchical levels of the data at different time scales, and hierarchical generative models are valuable theoretical tools for understanding data structure.
papers.key_findings:
At small inversion times, only low-level features change and the class remains the same.
There is a characteristic time scale where the class undergoes a sudden transition.
Even after the class transition, low-level features can persist and compose the new image.
Theoretical analysis with a hierarchical generative model (Random Hierarchy Model) predicts these observations using belief propagation.
Internal representations of deep convolutional networks reflect the hierarchical structure, with early layer similarities changing smoothly and logits showing a sharp transition.
future_direction: Investigating whether U-Nets approximate belief propagation.
Using deep hierarchical segmentation techniques to extract latent variables for testing predictions.
Testing predictions on other modalities such as language and biological structures.
papers.abstract: Understanding the structure of real data is paramount in advancing modern deep-learning methodologies. Natural data such as images are believed to be composed of features organized in a hierarchical and combinatorial manner, which neural networks capture during learning. Recent advancements show that diffusion models can generate high-quality images, hinting at their ability to capture this underlying compositional structure. We study this phenomenon in a hierarchical generative model of data. We find that the backward diffusion process acting after a time $t$ is governed by a phase transition at some threshold time, where the probability of reconstructing high-level features, like the class of an image, suddenly drops. Instead, the reconstruction of low-level features, such as specific details of an image, evolves smoothly across the whole diffusion process. This result implies that at times beyond the transition, the class has changed, but the generated sample may still be composed of low-level elements of the initial image. We validate these theoretical insights through numerical experiments on class-unconditional ImageNet diffusion models. Our analysis characterizes the relationship between time and scale in diffusion models and puts forward generative models as powerful tools to model combinatorial data properties.

papers.title: Interpretability for Time Series Transformers using A Concept Bottleneck Framework
papers.research_question: How can we make time series transformers interpretable by steering them to learn predefined, interpretable concepts while maintaining forecasting performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models and Centered Kernel Alignment to steer time series transformers to learn predefined interpretable concepts (e.g., a linear surrogate model and time features) in a designated bottleneck layer, improving interpretability without significantly harming forecasting performance.
papers.conclusion: The concept bottleneck framework successfully improves the interpretability of time series transformers by encouraging specific components to align with human-understandable concepts, with minimal impact on forecasting accuracy, and enables faithful local interventions.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework maintains model performance (MSE, MAE) on benchmark datasets while making the bottleneck layer's representations highly similar to the predefined concepts, as measured by CKA.
Component visualizations and activation patching interventions confirm that the bottleneck components learn and causally influence the model's predictions based on the intended concepts.
The framework is successfully applied to three different transformer architectures (Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer, FEDformer) on synthetic and real-world time series data.
Including a 'free' component in the bottleneck (not constrained by concepts) can help maintain performance and capture additional, non-predefined patterns in the data.
The intervention experiment demonstrates that the model's performance on time-shifted data can be restored by patching the activations of the time-concept component, confirming the causal role of the bottleneck.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes that relevant, interpretable concepts are known a priori and provided to the model.
The framework introduces additional computational cost during training due to the CKA loss calculation.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other types of sequential data beyond time series.
Exploring more complex or domain-specific interpretable concepts.
Investigating the use of the framework for model debugging and out-of-distribution robustness.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability focuses on reverse engineering the internal mechanisms learned by neural networks. We extend our focus and propose to mechanistically forward engineer using our framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models. In the context of long-term time series forecasting, we modify the training objective to encourage a model to develop representations which are similar to predefined, interpretable concepts using Centered Kernel Alignment. This steers the bottleneck components to learn the predefined concepts, while allowing other components to learn other, undefined concepts. We apply the framework to the Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer and FEDformer, and present an in-depth analysis on synthetic data and on a variety of benchmark datasets. We find that the model performance remains mostly unaffected, while the model shows much improved interpretability. Additionally, we verify the interpretation of the bottleneck components with an intervention experiment using activation patching.

papers.title: Prototype Generation: Robust Feature Visualisation for Data Independent Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can a robust feature visualization method generate prototypes with natural internal activations to provide trustworthy, data-independent interpretability and reveal model biases?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Prototype Generation, a robust feature visualization method that produces prototypes with natural internal activation paths, enabling data-independent identification of model biases and spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: Prototype Generation is a robust feature visualization method that provides trustworthy, data-independent insights into model behavior, useful for identifying biases and failure modes to improve model performance and fairness.
papers.key_findings:
Prototypes generated by the method have higher path similarity to natural images than previous feature visualization methods.
The method can identify biases in models, such as Resnet-18's bias towards lighter-skinned faces in the 'academic gown' class.
The method can identify spurious correlations, such as Resnet-18 misclassifying mortarboards with faces as academic gowns.
The method provides insights without requiring a test set, offering a data-independent approach to interpretability.
Prototypes can be used for iterative model improvement by revealing what the model has learned or failed to learn.
papers.limitation: No formal proof that feature visualisation will consistently offer useful insights across all use cases and models; the issue of fooling circuits is not addressed.
future_direction: Address the limitations regarding formal guarantees and fooling circuits.
Expand analysis with further case studies of real-world deployed models for bias detection and knowledge discovery.
Apply prototype generation to other modalities such as tabular data and language.
papers.abstract: We introduce Prototype Generation, a stricter and more robust form of feature visualisation for model-agnostic, data-independent interpretability of image classification models. We demonstrate its ability to generate inputs that result in natural activation paths, countering previous claims that feature visualisation algorithms are untrustworthy due to the unnatural internal activations. We substantiate these claims by quantitatively measuring similarity between the internal activations of our generated prototypes and natural images. We also demonstrate how the interpretation of generated prototypes yields important insights, highlighting spurious correlations and biases learned by models which quantitative methods over test-sets cannot identify.

papers.title: How Well do Feature Visualizations Support Causal Understanding of CNN\n Activations?
papers.research_question: Do synthetic feature visualizations (activation maximization) provide humans with better causal understanding of CNN unit activations compared to other visualization methods like natural dataset samples?
papers.core_contribution: Synthetic feature visualizations do not provide a substantial advantage over simple alternative visualizations (e.g., natural dataset samples) in helping humans gain causal understanding of CNN activations, as measured by a psychophysical task where participants predict the effect of image occlusions on unit activations.
papers.conclusion: Feature visualizations do not offer a meaningful advantage over simpler alternatives for causal understanding of CNN activations, and the proposed psychophysical task serves as a quantitative benchmark for future interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
Synthetic feature visualizations yield 68±4% accuracy, only slightly above the 60±3% baseline with no visualizations and not significantly higher than other visualizations (66±3% to 67±3%).
Simple heuristics (e.g., choosing the image with an unoccluded center or lower variance) can achieve similar performance (up to 63%) without any reference visualizations.
There is no evidence that the widely-used feature visualization method by Olah et al. provides better causal understanding than natural dataset examples or other alternatives.
Human performance and strategy agreement (measured by Cohen's kappa) are only moderate, indicating room for subjective decisions.
The proposed psychophysical task provides an objective benchmark for evaluating unit-level interpretability methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a single network architecture (InceptionV1) and a single task (image classification).
The two-alternative forced choice task is a simplified version of counterfactual reasoning and may not capture all aspects of causality.
future_direction: Adapt the psychophysical task to account for other notions of causality and interpretability.
Extend the evaluation to other network architectures and tasks.
Use the task as a challenging test case to steer further development of feature visualizations.
papers.abstract:
A precise understanding of why units in an artificial network respond to
certain stimuli would constitute a big step towards explainable artificial
intelligence. One widely used approach towards this goal is to visualize unit
responses via activation maximization. These synthetic feature visualizations
are purported to provide humans with precise information about the image
features that cause a unit to be activated - an advantage over other
alternatives like strongly activating natural dataset samples. If humans indeed
gain causal insight from visualizations, this should enable them to predict the
effect of an intervention, such as how occluding a certain patch of the image
(say, a dog's head) changes a unit's activation. Here, we test this hypothesis
by asking humans to decide which of two square occlusions causes a larger
change to a unit's activation. Both a large-scale crowdsourced experiment and
measurements with experts show that on average the extremely activating feature
visualizations by Olah et al. (2017) indeed help humans on this task ($68 \pm
4$% accuracy; baseline performance without any visualizations is $60 \pm 3$%).
However, they do not provide any substantial advantage over other
visualizations (such as e.g. dataset samples), which yield similar performance
($66\pm3$% to $67 \pm3$% accuracy). Taken together, we propose an objective
psychophysical task to quantify the benefit of unit-level interpretability
methods for humans, and find no evidence that a widely-used feature
visualization method provides humans with better "causal understanding" of unit
activations than simple alternative visualizations.

papers.title: Position-aware Automatic Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can circuit discovery methods be improved to incorporate positional information, addressing the limitation of position-invariant assumptions in existing methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces position-aware edge attribution patching (PEAP) and dataset schemas to enable automatic discovery of position-sensitive circuits in language models, improving the trade-off between circuit size and faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: The proposed position-aware circuit discovery method with schemas provides a more precise and automated approach to understanding model mechanisms, offering better faithfulness and size trade-offs.
papers.key_findings:
PEAP yields smaller and more faithful circuits compared to position-agnostic methods, as demonstrated on tasks like Greater-Than and IOI.
Schemas allow position-aware circuit discovery for variable-length inputs by defining semantic spans across examples.
Automated schema generation using LLMs, enhanced with saliency scores, produces schemas comparable to human-designed ones in terms of circuit faithfulness.
Position-aware circuits reduce cancellation and overestimation effects that occur when aggregating edge scores across positions without differentiation.
future_direction: Relax the sequential order assumption in schemas to support greater variation across examples.
papers.abstract: A widely used strategy to discover and understand language model mechanisms is circuit analysis. A circuit is a minimal subgraph of a model's computation graph that executes a specific task. We identify a gap in existing circuit discovery methods: they assume circuits are position-invariant, treating model components as equally relevant across input positions. This limits their ability to capture cross-positional interactions or mechanisms that vary across positions. To address this gap, we propose two improvements to incorporate positionality into circuits, even on tasks containing variable-length examples. First, we extend edge attribution patching, a gradient-based method for circuit discovery, to differentiate between token positions. Second, we introduce the concept of a dataset schema, which defines token spans with similar semantics across examples, enabling position-aware circuit discovery in datasets with variable length examples. We additionally develop an automated pipeline for schema generation and application using large language models. Our approach enables fully automated discovery of position-sensitive circuits, yielding better trade-offs between circuit size and faithfulness compared to prior work.

papers.title: How Well do Feature Visualizations Support Causal Understanding of CNN Activations?
papers.research_question: Do synthetic feature visualizations provide humans with better causal understanding of unit activations in CNNs compared to alternative visualizations like natural dataset samples?
papers.core_contribution: Synthetic feature visualizations by Olah et al. provide only a small improvement over no visualizations and no significant advantage over natural dataset samples in a psychophysical task measuring causal understanding of CNN unit activations.
papers.conclusion: Feature visualizations do not provide better causal understanding than simple alternatives like natural dataset samples, and the proposed psychophysical task serves as a benchmark for evaluating interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
Synthetic feature visualizations yield 68% accuracy in a human psychophysical task, but natural references yield 66-67% accuracy, showing no substantial advantage.
Without any visualizations, human accuracy is 60%.
Simple baselines (e.g., center or variance heuristics) can reach similar performance (up to 63% accuracy).
There is systematic but fairly low agreement (Cohen's kappa up to 0.40) between participants and between participants and baselines.
The results suggest that all tested visualization methods are similarly helpful for humans in predicting the effect of interventions on unit activations.
papers.limitation:
The experiment only tests one specific notion of causality (predicting the effect of an occlusion intervention).
The task is simplified to a two-alternative forced choice, which may not capture all aspects of causal understanding.
The results are based on a specific network (InceptionV1) and a limited set of units and images, which may not generalize.
future_direction: Adapt the psychophysical task to account for other notions of causality and interpretability.
Use the task as a challenging test case to steer further development of feature visualizations.
papers.abstract: A precise understanding of why units in an artificial network respond to certain stimuli would constitute a big step towards explainable artificial intelligence. One widely used approach towards this goal is to visualize unit responses via activation maximization. These synthetic feature visualizations are purported to provide humans with precise information about the image features that cause a unit to be activated - an advantage over other alternatives like strongly activating natural dataset samples. If humans indeed gain causal insight from visualizations, this should enable them to predict the effect of an intervention, such as how occluding a certain patch of the image (say, a dog's head) changes a unit's activation. Here, we test this hypothesis by asking humans to decide which of two square occlusions causes a larger change to a unit's activation. Both a large-scale crowdsourced experiment and measurements with experts show that on average the extremely activating feature visualizations by Olah et al. (2017) indeed help humans on this task ($68 \pm 4$% accuracy; baseline performance without any visualizations is $60 \pm 3$%). However, they do not provide any substantial advantage over other visualizations (such as e.g. dataset samples), which yield similar performance ($66\pm3$% to $67 \pm3$% accuracy). Taken together, we propose an objective psychophysical task to quantify the benefit of unit-level interpretability methods for humans, and find no evidence that a widely-used feature visualization method provides humans with better "causal understanding" of unit activations than simple alternative visualizations.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be used to interpret the internal mechanisms of neural NLP models, specifically to understand the role of individual components (like neurons and attention heads) in mediating gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structural-behavioral framework based on causal mediation analysis for interpreting neural NLP models, and applies it to gender bias, revealing that bias effects are sparse, synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis provides a useful framework for interpreting neural NLP models, offering insights into the internal mechanisms by which properties like gender bias flow from input to output through various model components.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias effects are sparse, concentrated in a relatively small number of model components (neurons and attention heads).
Gender bias effects are synergistic, with different model components interacting to amplify or repress their individual effects.
Gender bias effects are decomposable, with the total effect approximating the sum of direct and indirect effects, despite model non-linearity.
Larger models tend to exhibit larger gender bias effects.
The causal mediation analysis framework captures general patterns of causal structure in Transformer architectures, not just model-specific characteristics.
papers.limitation:
The experimental design focuses on gender bias in a binary setup, which does not account for a gender-inclusive spectrum.
Preliminary experiments with gender-neutral references (e.g., singular 'they') showed models have not learned these concepts well, and the setup suffers from confounders like plural 'they'.
Results for masked language models (e.g., BERT) are less clear, potentially due to differences in scoring multi-token continuations compared to autoregressive models.
future_direction: Applying the methodology to more gender-inclusive setups and other kinds of biases.
Using mediation analysis to guide the development of new debiasing methods that establish counterfactual fairness.
Exploring path-specific effects to identify exact mechanisms through which biases arise.
papers.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoder as a Zero-Shot Classifier for Concept Erasing in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How to precisely erase unwanted concepts in text-to-image diffusion models while preserving overall performance, and how to do so in an expandable way without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Interpret-then-Deactivate (ItD), a framework that uses a sparse autoencoder to interpret concepts as combinations of features and deactivates only features unique to target concepts, enabling precise and expandable concept erasure without retraining the diffusion model.
papers.conclusion: ItD is a simple and effective approach to erase target concepts while maintaining diverse remaining concepts, and it is robust against adversarial attacks.
papers.key_findings:
ItD effectively erases target concepts (celebrities, artistic styles, explicit content) while preserving the generation quality of remaining concepts.
ItD is robust against adversarial prompts designed to circumvent content filters.
ItD can erase multiple concepts without requiring additional training.
ItD outperforms existing baselines in preserving remaining concepts, as shown by quantitative metrics.
papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have achieved remarkable progress in generating high-quality images but also raise people's concerns about generating harmful or misleading content. While extensive approaches have been proposed to erase unwanted concepts without requiring retraining from scratch, they inadvertently degrade performance on normal generation tasks. In this work, we propose Interpret then Deactivate (ItD), a novel framework to enable precise concept removal in T2I diffusion models while preserving overall performance. ItD first employs a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to interpret each concept as a combination of multiple features. By permanently deactivating the specific features associated with target concepts, we repurpose SAE as a zero-shot classifier that identifies whether the input prompt includes target concepts, allowing selective concept erasure in diffusion models. Moreover, we demonstrate that ItD can be easily extended to erase multiple concepts without requiring further training. Comprehensive experiments across celebrity identities, artistic styles, and explicit content demonstrate ItD's effectiveness in eliminating targeted concepts without interfering with normal concept generation. Additionally, ItD is also robust against adversarial prompts designed to circumvent content filters. Code is available at: https://github.com/NANSirun/Interpret-then-deactivate.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Enabling Local Editing in Diffusion Models by Joint and Individual Component Analysis
papers.research_question: How to achieve local image editing in diffusion models by factorizing the latent semantics of the denoising network into joint and individual components.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method for local image editing in diffusion models by decomposing the Jacobian of the denoising network into joint and individual components, enabling localized semantic manipulations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method enables localized semantic manipulation of real images using pre-trained diffusion models by factorizing latent subspaces, with discovered directions generalizing across images and outperforming previous methods.
papers.key_findings:
The method identifies semantic directions in the latent space that are localized to specific image regions, enabling fine-grained editing.
Decomposing the Jacobian into joint and individual components disentangles global and local variations, allowing for edits that affect only the region of interest.
The discovered latent directions generalize from a single reference image to other images, making the method suitable for plug-and-play applications.
The method produces edits with higher fidelity and better localization compared to existing state-of-the-art alternatives, as measured by FID, ID, and ROIR metrics.
future_direction: Explore the latent semantics of video diffusion models.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Diffusion Models (DMs) have led to significant progress in visual synthesis and editing tasks, establishing them as a strong competitor to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). However, the latent space of DMs is not as well understood as that of GANs. Recent research has focused on unsupervised semantic discovery in the latent space of DMs by leveraging the bottleneck layer of the denoising network, which has been shown to exhibit properties of a semantic latent space. However, these approaches are limited to discovering global attributes. In this paper we address, the challenge of local image manipulation in DMs and introduce an unsupervised method to factorize the latent semantics learned by the denoising network of pre-trained DMs. Given an arbitrary image and defined regions of interest, we utilize the Jacobian of the denoising network to establish a relation between the regions of interest and their corresponding subspaces in the latent space. Furthermore, we disentangle the joint and individual components of these subspaces to identify latent directions that enable local image manipulation. Once discovered, these directions can be applied to different images to produce semantically consistent edits, making our method suitable for practical applications. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that our method can produce semantic edits that are more localized and have better fidelity compared to the state-of-the-art.

papers.title: Diffusion Lens: Interpreting Text Encoders in Text-to-Image Pipelines
papers.research_question: How does the text encoder in text-to-image diffusion models internally process prompts, specifically regarding conceptual combination and memory retrieval?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DIFFUSION LENS, a method to visualize intermediate representations of text encoders in T2I models, and uses it to reveal how conceptual combination and memory retrieval are processed gradually across layers.
papers.conclusion: The DIFFUSION LENS provides a new method to interpret text encoders in T2I models, revealing gradual processes in conceptual combination and memory retrieval, and opens up future applications for model analysis and improvement.
papers.key_findings:
Complex prompts describing multiple objects are composed progressively and require more computation compared to simple prompts.
Uncommon concepts (e.g., rare animals) require further computation and emerge gradually across layers, while common concepts emerge early.
Early layers act as a 'bag of concepts', encoding individual concepts without relations, which emerge in later layers.
The order of object emergence is influenced by linear order in CLIP and syntactic precedence in T5.
Fine details, such as facial features of celebrities, materialize at later layers.
papers.limitation:
Limited number of publicly available and open source T2I models and their text encoders.
Experiments mostly used automatically generated prompts, which are less complex than human-written prompts.
DIFFUSION LENS requires annotation to derive large-scale conclusions, as images need to be evaluated.
future_direction: Extending the method to interpret other language models, whether or not they are used in T2I pipelines.
Identifying points of failure in the computation process or removing undesired traits from early layers.
Visualizing individual sub-block components such as MLPs, attention heads, and residual connections.
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models (T2I) use a latent representation of a text prompt to guide the image generation process. However, the process by which the encoder produces the text representation is unknown. We propose the Diffusion Lens, a method for analyzing the text encoder of T2I models by generating images from its intermediate representations. Using the Diffusion Lens, we perform an extensive analysis of two recent T2I models. Exploring compound prompts, we find that complex scenes describing multiple objects are composed progressively and more slowly compared to simple scenes; Exploring knowledge retrieval, we find that representation of uncommon concepts requires further computation compared to common concepts, and that knowledge retrieval is gradual across layers. Overall, our findings provide valuable insights into the text encoder component in T2I pipelines.

papers.title: Attacks Meet Interpretability: Attribute-steered Detection of\n Adversarial Samples
papers.research_question: How can we detect adversarial samples in face recognition models by leveraging the interpretability of DNNs, specifically by examining whether model predictions are based on human-perceptible attributes?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel adversarial sample detection technique for face recognition models based on interpretability, featuring bi-directional correspondence inference between face attributes and internal neurons, and neuron strengthening/weakening.
papers.conclusion: AmI is an effective adversarial sample detection technique for face recognition models that leverages interpretability through bi-directional attribute-neuron correspondence inference and model transformation.
papers.key_findings:
AmI achieves 94% detection accuracy for 7 different adversarial attacks with 9.91% false positives on benign inputs, outperforming the state-of-the-art feature squeezing technique.
Bi-directional reasoning (attribute substitution and preservation) is critical for extracting high-quality attribute witnesses and achieving good detection performance.
The technique is robust to the exclusion of witnesses for individual attributes, with detection accuracy degrading by less than 5% in most cases.
Attribute-steered model transformation (neuron strengthening and weakening) effectively amplifies the reasoning part of the computation and suppresses the uninterpretable part for detection.
The extracted attribute witnesses are of high quality, achieving higher accuracy in attribute detection than using the face descriptor layer of VGG-Face.
papers.abstract:
Adversarial sample attacks perturb benign inputs to induce DNN misbehaviors.
Recent research has demonstrated the widespread presence and the devastating
consequences of such attacks. Existing defense techniques either assume prior
knowledge of specific attacks or may not work well on complex models due to
their underlying assumptions. We argue that adversarial sample attacks are
deeply entangled with interpretability of DNN models: while classification
results on benign inputs can be reasoned based on the human perceptible
features/attributes, results on adversarial samples can hardly be explained.
Therefore, we propose a novel adversarial sample detection technique for face
recognition models, based on interpretability. It features a novel
bi-directional correspondence inference between attributes and internal neurons
to identify neurons critical for individual attributes. The activation values
of critical neurons are enhanced to amplify the reasoning part of the
