Develop more comprehensive metrics that capture other aspects of interpretability.
Extend the benchmark to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? In pursuit of lasting evaluation standards, we propose MIB, a Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark, with two tracks spanning four tasks and five models. MIB favors methods that precisely and concisely recover relevant causal pathways or causal variables in neural language models. The circuit localization track compares methods that locate the model components - and connections between them - most important for performing a task (e.g., attribution patching or information flow routes). The causal variable localization track compares methods that featurize a hidden vector, e.g., sparse autoencoders (SAEs) or distributed alignment search (DAS), and align those features to a task-relevant causal variable. Using MIB, we find that attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization. For causal variable localization, we find that the supervised DAS method performs best, while SAE features are not better than neurons, i.e., non-featurized hidden vectors. These findings illustrate that MIB enables meaningful comparisons, and increases our confidence that there has been real progress in the field.

papers.title: Dissecting and Mitigating Diffusion Bias via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate social biases in diffusion models by identifying and manipulating the internal decision-making mechanisms (bias features) that causally drive biased outputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces DIFFLENS, a mechanistic interpretability framework that identifies intrinsic bias features within diffusion models and enables fine-grained control over bias levels in generated content by directly manipulating these features.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel mechanistic interpretability approach to understand and mitigate bias in diffusion models, offering precise control over bias generation and insights into the model's internal decision-making processes.
papers.key_findings:
The paper identifies specific internal features (bias features) within diffusion models that causally drive the generation of biased content.
The proposed DIFFLENS method effectively mitigates social biases (e.g., gender, age, race) in generated images while preserving image quality and semantic coherence.
DIFFLENS allows for precise, fine-grained control over the level of bias in generated outputs by scaling or suppressing the identified bias features.
Different discovered bias features control distinct fine-grained aspects of generation (e.g., hair style for gender).
The method demonstrates effectiveness on both unconditional and conditional diffusion models across multiple social attributes.
papers.limitation:
The definition and evaluation of social bias are complex and inherently challenging, particularly for attributes like race, leading to potential instability in results.
The sparse autoencoder features may not fully align with human-interpretable concepts, as bias attributes are compound concepts that may relate to multiple features.
The approach treats debiased attributes as discrete categories (e.g., male/female), overlooking individuals who do not fit traditional classifications (e.g., non-binary gender or mixed race).
future_direction: Better alignment of sparse autoencoder features with human-interpretable concepts.
Addressing the representation of non-binary and mixed-race individuals in bias mitigation.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated impressive capabilities in synthesizing diverse content. However, despite their high-quality outputs, these models often perpetuate social biases, including those related to gender and race. These biases can potentially contribute to harmful real-world consequences, reinforcing stereotypes and exacerbating inequalities in various social contexts. While existing research on diffusion bias mitigation has predominantly focused on guiding content generation, it often neglects the intrinsic mechanisms within diffusion models that causally drive biased outputs. In this paper, we investigate the internal processes of diffusion models, identifying specific decision-making mechanisms, termed bias features, embedded within the model architecture. By directly manipulating these features, our method precisely isolates and adjusts the elements responsible for bias generation, permitting granular control over the bias levels in the generated content. Through experiments on both unconditional and conditional diffusion models across various social bias attributes, we demonstrate our method's efficacy in managing generation distribution while preserving image quality. We also dissect the discovered model mechanism, revealing different intrinsic features controlling fine-grained aspects of generation, boosting further research on mechanistic interpretability of diffusion models.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Trade-Offs in Fine-Tuned Diffusion Models between Accuracy and Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does fine-tuning diffusion models with a learnable text encoder affect their interpretability, and what is the trade-off between image fidelity and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning diffusion models with a learnable text encoder improves image quality but destroys interpretability (localization ability), while freezing the text encoder retains interpretability at a slight cost to image quality, revealing a trade-off.
papers.conclusion: The standard practice of fine-tuning diffusion models with a learnable text encoder leads to a loss of interpretability; freezing the text encoder preserves interpretability while maintaining reasonable generative performance, highlighting an important design consideration.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning diffusion models with a learnable text encoder (Finetune L) yields high image quality (low FID) but poor interpretability (low localization metrics).
Fine-tuning with a frozen text encoder (Finetune F) retains strong interpretability (good localization) but results in slightly worse image quality.
The variability of text prompts impacts interpretability; higher variability (full impressions) leads to better interpretability than low variability (class labels).
The end-of-string (EOS) token often shows high localization performance, but only the frozen model learns to associate disease-describing tokens with correct image regions.
The trade-off between image fidelity and interpretability is demonstrated, suggesting interpretability should be considered when designing generative models for critical domains like medical imaging.
papers.limitation: FID has its own limitation due to it being a trained metric and requiring too many samples to be accurate, and conditional generation evaluation is limited as there is no ground-truth data available.
future_direction: Perform a large-scale study that analyses the quality of images judged by domain experts in relation to FID and CNR to see which metric better captures generative quality.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in diffusion models have significantly impacted the trajectory of generative machine learning re-search, with many adopting the strategy of fine-tuning pre-trained models using domain-specific text-to-image datasets. Notably, this method has been readily employed for medical applications, such as X-ray image synthesis, leveraging the plethora of associated radiology reports. Yet, a prevailing concern is the lack of assurance on whether these models genuinely comprehend their generated content. With the evolution of text conditional image generation, these models have grown potent enough to facilitate object localization scrutiny. Our research underscores this advancement in the critical realm of medical imaging, emphasizing the crucial role of interpretability. We further unravel a consequential trade-off between image fidelity – as gauged by conventional metrics – and model interpretability in generative diffusion models. Specifically, the adoption of learnable text encoders when fine-tuning results in diminished interpretability. Our in-depth exploration uncovers the underlying factors responsible for this divergence. Consequently, we present a set of design principles for the development of truly interpretable generative models. Code is available at https://github.com/MischaD/chest-distillation.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: Interpretable Diffusion Models with B-cos Networks
papers.research_question: How can text-to-image diffusion models be made inherently interpretable to provide insight into how individual prompt tokens affect the generated image?
papers.core_contribution: This paper integrates B-cos networks into text-to-image diffusion models, providing inherent interpretability and token-level attributions that link output pixels to prompt tokens, enabling the detection of missing concepts in generated images.
papers.conclusion: B-cos networks can be effectively used in text-to-image diffusion models to provide inherent interpretability, with explanations that faithfully capture the alignment between an image and its prompt, enabling the detection of missing concepts.
papers.key_findings:
B-cos networks can be effectively integrated into diffusion models, providing faithful explanations of prompt-image alignment.
The proposed method yields token-level attributions that consistently assign higher relevance scores to semantically meaningful tokens.
The explanations can identify failure cases where the generated image does not align with the prompt, such as a missing object.
The model summary (dynamic linear transformation) effectively captures the underlying computations, as shown by the close match between normalized reconstructions and model outputs.
Using deterministic sampling (DDIM with σ=0) avoids introducing biases that would break the completeness of the B-cos summary.
papers.limitation: The approach currently leads to reduced generative performance (lower image quality) compared to standard diffusion models.
future_direction: Developing methods to overcome the trade-off between interpretability and generative performance.
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models generate images by iteratively denoising random noise, conditioned on a prompt. While these models have enabled impressive progress in image generation, they often fail to accurately reflect all semantic information described in the prompt -- failures that are difficult to detect automatically. In this work, we introduce a diffusion model architecture built with B-cos modules that offers inherent interpretability. Our approach provides insight into how individual prompt tokens affect the generated image by producing explanations that highlight the pixel regions influenced by each token. We demonstrate that B-cos diffusion models can produce high-quality images while providing meaningful insights into prompt-image alignment.

papers.title: Beyond the Black Box: Identifiable Interpretation and Control in Generative Models via Causal Minimality
papers.research_question: Under what theoretical conditions can we reliably identify meaningful, interpretable latent concepts within modern generative models? And what actionable, theoretically-grounded insights can advance both interpretability and controllability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a theoretical framework based on causal minimality that provides conditions under which latent representations in generative models can be identified component-wise, enabling interpretable hierarchical concept graphs and fine-grained control.
papers.conclusion: The experiments illustrate the implications of the theorems and show how a principled, causal understanding can guide the application of established interpretation techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The principle of causal minimality, instantiated as sparsity constraints, enables the extraction of interpretable hierarchical concept graphs from text-to-image diffusion models.
The learned representations under these conditions are component-wise identifiable, meaning they correspond to true latent variables of the data-generating process.
These causally grounded concepts allow for fine-grained model steering, demonstrated in tasks like model unlearning, controllable generation, and multi-level editing.
papers.limitation: The theoretical assumptions, such as causal minimality and smoothness, may not hold universally in practice.
papers.abstract: Deep generative models, while revolutionizing fields like image and text generation, largely operate as opaque black boxes, hindering human understanding, control, and alignment. While methods like sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show remarkable empirical success, they often lack theoretical guarantees, risking subjective insights. Our primary objective is to establish a principled foundation for interpretable generative models. We demonstrate that the principle of causal minimality -- favoring the simplest causal explanation -- can endow the latent representations of diffusion vision and autoregressive language models with clear causal interpretation and robust, component-wise identifiable control. We introduce a novel theoretical framework for hierarchical selection models, where higher-level concepts emerge from the constrained composition of lower-level variables, better capturing the complex dependencies in data generation. Under theoretically derived minimality conditions (manifesting as sparsity or compression constraints), we show that learned representations can be equivalent to the true latent variables of the data-generating process. Empirically, applying these constraints to leading generative models allows us to extract their innate hierarchical concept graphs, offering fresh insights into their internal knowledge organization. Furthermore, these causally grounded concepts serve as levers for fine-grained model steering, paving the way for transparent, reliable systems.

papers.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like molecules capture the rules of molecular representation and maintain syntactic and chemical validity during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a mechanistic analysis of an autoregressive transformer trained on drug-like molecules, identifying specialized circuits for syntactic and chemical validity and using sparse autoencoders to extract chemically meaningful features that enhance downstream predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: Molecular transformers develop specialized mechanisms for maintaining syntactic and chemical validity, and sparse autoencoders can disentangle these representations into interpretable features that are useful for downstream tasks and controllable generation.
papers.key_findings:
Identification of attention heads that implement ring and branch syntax circuits, with a division of labor between pointer and writer heads for ring closure.
Discovery of a linearly decodable valence capacity representation in the residual stream that can be steered to modulate bond predictions.
Extraction of sparse feature dictionaries via SAEs that align with chemically meaningful substructures, enabled by an automated fragment-screening pipeline.
Demonstration that SAE-derived features improve transformer embeddings on property prediction tasks, competitive with traditional fingerprints.
SAE features can be used for steering generation towards desired chemical structures.
papers.limitation: Steering with SAE features can degrade validity for complex targets and the effects are not uniform, indicating that SAE latents are preliminary control knobs rather than fully-fledged conditional generators.
papers.abstract: Transformers generate valid and diverse chemical structures, but little is known about the mechanisms that enable these models to capture the rules of molecular representation. We present a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like small molecules to reveal the computational structure underlying their capabilities across multiple levels of abstraction. We identify computational patterns consistent with low-level syntactic parsing and more abstract chemical validity constraints. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we extract feature dictionaries associated with chemically relevant activation patterns. We validate our findings on downstream tasks and find that mechanistic insights can translate to predictive performance in various practical settings.

papers.title: TIDE : Temporal-Aware Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Diffusion Transformers in Image Generation
papers.research_question: How can we extract sparse, interpretable activation features across timesteps in Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) to understand their internal mechanisms and enable controllability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TIDE, a temporal-aware sparse autoencoder framework for extracting interpretable features from Diffusion Transformers, revealing hierarchical semantic representations and enabling applications like safe image editing.
papers.conclusion: TIDE provides a sparse, temporally-aware interpretability framework for DiTs, enabling transparent analysis and practical applications like image editing, laying a foundation for more trustworthy and controllable generative systems.
papers.key_findings:
TIDE effectively captures temporally-varying activation patterns in DiTs, improving reconstruction and generalization.
DiTs naturally learn hierarchical semantics (3D structure, object class, fine-grained concepts) during large-scale pre-training.
TIDE maintains generation quality (e.g., FID) while providing interpretable features, with minimal performance degradation.
The method generalizes across different diffusion backbones (SDXL, FLUX-dev).
TIDE enables safe image editing, achieving a low Attack Success Rate on the I2P benchmark.
papers.limitation: Current performance in complex editing scenarios remains limited by sparsity constraints.
future_direction: Explore more flexible sparse mechanisms to improve expressiveness.
papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are a powerful yet underexplored class of generative models compared to U-Net-based diffusion architectures. We propose TIDE-Temporal-aware sparse autoencoders for Interpretable Diffusion transformErs-a framework designed to extract sparse, interpretable activation features across timesteps in DiTs. TIDE effectively captures temporally-varying representations and reveals that DiTs naturally learn hierarchical semantics (e.g., 3D structure, object class, and fine-grained concepts) during large-scale pretraining. Experiments show that TIDE enhances interpretability and controllability while maintaining reasonable generation quality, enabling applications such as safe image editing and style transfer.

papers.title: Editing Implicit Assumptions in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can specific implicit assumptions in a text-to-image diffusion model be edited after training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TIME, a method to edit implicit assumptions in text-to-image diffusion models by updating the projection matrices in cross-attention layers, and introduces the TIMED dataset for evaluation.
papers.conclusion: TIME is an efficient method for editing implicit assumptions in text-to-image models and the introduced dataset will help pave the way for future advances in model editing.
papers.key_findings:
TIME successfully edits the model with high efficacy (88.10%) and generality (69.04%) on the TIMED dataset.
TIME exhibits a trade-off between generality and specificity, controllable via the hyperparameter λ.
TIME can reduce gender bias in professions, moving the gender distribution towards equality.
The method is efficient, modifying only 2.2% of the diffusion model parameters in under one second.
The edit generalizes to related prompts while leaving unrelated generations mostly unaffected.
papers.limitation:
TIME inherits the generative limitations of the base model (e.g., compositionality or counting failures).
TIME sometimes applies an edit too mildly (hindering generality) or too aggressively (hindering specificity).
Editing multiple assumptions at once is difficult as debiasing one profession affects the gender ratio of others.
future_direction: Analyze the role of different components in storing and retrieving knowledge within the cross-attention mechanism.
Expand the method for editing multiple facts in bulk while maintaining the model's performance.
Further investigate gender bias mitigation towards a more comprehensive debiasing method.
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models often make implicit assumptions about the world when generating images. While some assumptions are useful (e.g., the sky is blue), they can also be outdated, incorrect, or reflective of social biases present in the training data. Thus, there is a need to control these assumptions without requiring explicit user input or costly re-training. In this work, we aim to edit a given implicit assumption in a pre-trained diffusion model. Our Text-to-Image Model Editing method, TIME for short, receives a pair of inputs: a "source" under-specified prompt for which the model makes an implicit assumption (e.g., "a pack of roses"), and a "destination" prompt that describes the same setting, but with a specified desired attribute (e.g., "a pack of blue roses"). TIME then updates the model's cross-attention layers, as these layers assign visual meaning to textual tokens. We edit the projection matrices in these layers such that the source prompt is projected close to the destination prompt. Our method is highly efficient, as it modifies a mere 2.2% of the model's parameters in under one second. To evaluate model editing approaches, we introduce TIMED (TIME Dataset), containing 147 source and destination prompt pairs from various domains. Our experiments (using Stable Diffusion) show that TIME is successful in model editing, generalizes well for related prompts unseen during editing, and imposes minimal effect on unrelated generations.

papers.title: Exploring the Representation Manifolds of Stable Diffusion Through the Lens of Intrinsic Dimension
papers.research_question: How do prompts affect the intrinsic dimension of internal representations in Stable Diffusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that prompt choice significantly affects the intrinsic dimension of representations in Stable Diffusion, with correlation to prompt perplexity in bottleneck layers.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsic dimension could be a useful tool for future studies of the impact of different prompts on text-to-image models.
papers.key_findings:
Prompts have a substantial effect on the intrinsic dimension of internal representations, with variations up to 10 dimensions.
Intrinsic dimension in latent representations decreases monotonically during denoising, while in bottleneck representations it forms a U-shaped curve.
In bottleneck layers, intrinsic dimension correlates with prompt perplexity, suggesting that less likely prompts result in higher-dimensional representations.
The dynamics of intrinsic dimension over denoising steps depend on the layer from which representations are extracted.
The time step embedding vector contributes to the increase in intrinsic dimension in bottleneck representations at later denoising steps.
papers.limitation: The correlation between perplexity and intrinsic dimension must be treated with caution, as it is not observed in latent representations.
future_direction: Adapting the experiments to other text-to-image models like DALL-E.
Comparing perplexity scores with actual frequencies of prompt tokens in training data like LAION-5B.
More comprehensive studies of other models that utilize prompts.
papers.abstract: Prompting has become an important mechanism by which users can more effectively interact with many flavors of foundation model. Indeed, the last several years have shown that well-honed prompts can sometimes unlock emergent capabilities within such models. While there has been a substantial amount of empirical exploration of prompting within the community, relatively few works have studied prompting at a mathematical level. In this work we aim to take a first step towards understanding basic geometric properties induced by prompts in Stable Diffusion, focusing on the intrinsic dimension of internal representations within the model. We find that choice of prompt has a substantial impact on the intrinsic dimension of representations at both layers of the model which we explored, but that the nature of this impact depends on the layer being considered. For example, in certain bottleneck layers of the model, intrinsic dimension of representations is correlated with prompt perplexity (measured using a surrogate model), while this correlation is not apparent in the latent layers. Our evidence suggests that intrinsic dimension could be a useful tool for future studies of the impact of different prompts on text-to-image models.

papers.title: DLM-Scope: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be used for mechanistic interpretability in diffusion language models (DLMs), and how do their properties and applications differ from those in autoregressive LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for Diffusion Language Models (DLMs), demonstrating that SAEs can extract interpretable features, enable effective diffusion-time steering, analyze decoding order, and transfer from base to instruction-tuned models.
papers.conclusion: DLM-Scope establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows the great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on DLMs achieve a favorable sparsity-fidelity trade-off and can even reduce cross-entropy loss when inserted in early layers, a phenomenon absent or weaker in LLMs.
SAE features enable effective diffusion-time interventions (steering) that often outperform single-pass LLM steering.
SAE feature dynamics provide a useful signal for analyzing and correlating with the performance of different DLM decoding-order strategies.
Base-trained SAEs transfer almost losslessly to instruction-tuned DLMs in shallow and middle layers, but not in the deepest layer, indicating tuning-specific changes in deep representations.
future_direction: As DLMs scale, we plan to extend SAEs to more DLMs to better understand and improve models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a standard tool for mechanistic interpretability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs), enabling researchers to extract sparse, human-interpretable features and intervene on model behavior. Recently, as diffusion language models (DLMs) have become an increasingly promising alternative to the autoregressive LLMs, it is essential to develop tailored mechanistic interpretability tools for this emerging class of models. In this work, we present DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for DLMs, and demonstrate that trained Top-K SAEs can faithfully extract interpretable features. Notably, we find that inserting SAEs affects DLMs differently than autoregressive LLMs: while SAE insertion in LLMs typically incurs a loss penalty, in DLMs it can reduce cross-entropy loss when applied to early layers, a phenomenon absent or markedly weaker in LLMs. Additionally, SAE features in DLMs enable more effective diffusion-time interventions, often outperforming LLM steering. Moreover, we pioneer certain new SAE-based research directions for DLMs: we show that SAEs can provide useful signals for DLM decoding order; and the SAE features are stable during the post-training phase of DLMs. Our work establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows a great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.

papers.title: How Diffusion Models Learn to Factorize and Compose
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether and when diffusion models learn factorized representations of composable features, and how this relates to compositional generalization and interpolation abilities.
papers.core_contribution: Diffusion models learn factorized but not fully continuous representations of continuous features, enabling strong compositional generalization but limited interpolation. They can achieve compositionality with few compositional examples, and manifold formation relates to percolation theory.
papers.conclusion: Diffusion models learn factorized representations and can compositionally generalize given the full range of independent factors and a small amount of compositional examples, but fail under conditions such as unseen feature values, no compositional examples, insufficient data, or insufficient overlaps.
papers.key_findings:
Given factorized continuous conditional inputs, diffusion models learn 'hyper-factorized' representations orthogonal for independent features and different values of the same feature.
Models compose well but interpolate poorly; they can compositionally generalize when observing the full extent of each latent feature with few compositional examples.
Models trained on isolated factors require very few compositional examples to generalize, showing high data efficiency.
Formation of factorized representations requires a threshold amount of correlated data, related to percolation theory.
papers.limitation: The study uses simplified synthetic data (2D Gaussians), which may not fully capture the complexities of natural images and compositionality in real-world settings.
future_direction: Controlled experiments with data optimization for improving data efficiency using more realistic data.
Characterizing the connection between percolation theory and manifold formation in toy and realistic settings.
Extending percolation ideas to study phase transitions in other models like large language models.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models are capable of generating photo-realistic images that combine elements which likely do not appear together in the training set, demonstrating the ability to \textit{compositionally generalize}. Nonetheless, the precise mechanism of compositionality and how it is acquired through training remains elusive. Inspired by cognitive neuroscientific approaches, we consider a highly reduced setting to examine whether and when diffusion models learn semantically meaningful and factorized representations of composable features. We performed extensive controlled experiments on conditional Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) trained to generate various forms of 2D Gaussian bump images. We found that the models learn factorized but not fully continuous manifold representations for encoding continuous features of variation underlying the data. With such representations, models demonstrate superior feature compositionality but limited ability to interpolate over unseen values of a given feature. Our experimental results further demonstrate that diffusion models can attain compositionality with few compositional examples, suggesting a more efficient way to train DDPMs. Finally, we connect manifold formation in diffusion models to percolation theory in physics, offering insight into the sudden onset of factorized representation learning. Our thorough toy experiments thus contribute a deeper understanding of how diffusion models capture compositional structure in data.

papers.title: The Hidden Language of Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the internal representations of textual concepts in text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces CONCEPTOR, a method to decompose textual concepts in diffusion models into interpretable textual elements, revealing non-trivial structures in the learned representations such as visual connections, exemplar interpolations, and biases.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents CONCEPTOR, a method for interpreting concept representations in diffusion models, revealing non-trivial structures and biases, thus shedding light on the model's internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
CONCEPTOR decomposes concepts into a weighted combination of interpretable textual elements from the model's vocabulary.
It reveals visual connections between concepts that transcend their textual semantics (e.g., shape, texture, color).
Some concepts are represented as interpolations of exemplars (e.g., 'president' represented by famous presidents).
Homograph concepts can mix multiple meanings simultaneously in a single generated image.
CONCEPTOR can detect non-trivial social biases in concept representations that are not easily observable visually.
papers.limitation:
The visual impact of a decomposition element is not always completely aligned with its impact as a single token, as the effect depends on the context of the decomposition.
The method is limited to elements that are single tokens, so complex phrases cannot be included as a single element.
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have demonstrated an unparalleled ability to generate high-quality, diverse images from a textual prompt. However, the internal representations learned by these models remain an enigma. In this work, we present Conceptor, a novel method to interpret the internal representation of a textual concept by a diffusion model. This interpretation is obtained by decomposing the concept into a small set of human-interpretable textual elements. Applied over the state-of-the-art Stable Diffusion model, Conceptor reveals non-trivial structures in the representations of concepts. For example, we find surprising visual connections between concepts, that transcend their textual semantics. We additionally discover concepts that rely on mixtures of exemplars, biases, renowned artistic styles, or a simultaneous fusion of multiple meanings of the concept. Through a large battery of experiments, we demonstrate Conceptor's ability to provide meaningful, robust, and faithful decompositions for a wide variety of abstract, concrete, and complex textual concepts, while allowing to naturally connect each decomposition element to its corresponding visual impact on the generated images. Our code will be available at: https://hila-chefer.github.io/Conceptor/

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: ELROND: Exploring and decomposing intrinsic capabilities of diffusion models
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle semantic directions directly within the input embedding space of diffusion models to gain precise, unsupervised control over the visual variations generated from a single prompt?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ELROND, a framework that decomposes semantic concepts in diffusion models by analyzing gradients in the conditioning space, enabling precise steering, mitigating mode collapse, and providing a concept complexity metric.
papers.conclusion: ELROND provides a geometry-grounded method for interpreting and manipulating the generative capabilities of diffusion models without supervision.
papers.key_findings:
ELROND isolates interpretable, steerable directions for fine-grained control over a single concept.
It effectively mitigates mode collapse in distilled models by reintroducing lost diversity.
It establishes a novel estimator for concept complexity based on the dimensionality of the discovered subspace.
It enables token-level composability, allowing independent steering of distinct concepts within a complex scene.
It outperforms SliderSpace in generating diverse variations while maintaining similar text-to-image alignment.
papers.limitation:
The data collection phase is computationally extensive as extracting the gradient dataset requires backpropagating through the diffusion model for thousands of image pairs.
Some of the discovered directions might not be interpretable.
Adding some directions to a token may influence the visual realization of another token (semantic leaking).
papers.abstract: A single text prompt passed to a diffusion model often yields a wide range of visual outputs determined solely by stochastic process, leaving users with no direct control over which specific semantic variations appear in the image. While existing unsupervised methods attempt to analyze these variations via output features, they omit the underlying generative process. In this work, we propose a framework to disentangle these semantic directions directly within the input embedding space. To that end, we collect a set of gradients obtained by backpropagating the differences between stochastic realizations of a fixed prompt that we later decompose into meaningful steering directions with either Principal Components Analysis or Sparse Autoencoder. Our approach yields three key contributions: (1) it isolates interpretable, steerable directions for precise, fine-grained control over a single concept; (2) it effectively mitigates mode collapse in distilled models by reintroducing lost diversity; and (3) it establishes a novel estimator for concept complexity under a specific model, based on the dimensionality of the discovered subspace.

papers.title: Decoding Diffusion: A Scalable Framework for Unsupervised Analysis of Latent Space Biases and Representations Using Natural Language Prompts
papers.research_question: How to automatically map latent directions in diffusion models to semantic concepts using natural language prompts for scalable analysis of biases and representations?
papers.core_contribution: A framework for unsupervised exploration of diffusion model latent spaces by mapping latent directions to natural language prompts, enabling automatic interpretation and broad concept analysis.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a scalable and versatile tool for interpreting diffusion model latent spaces, contributing to more transparent, interpretable, and ethically responsible generative models.
papers.key_findings:
The framework identifies gender biases in diffusion models, with professions like pilot and construction worker showing stronger male stereotypes.
Cosine distance between gendered and gender-neutral prompts correlates with the likelihood of generating female-presenting images.
Clustering of h-space vectors from food captions reveals semantic groups like square dishes and pots with soup.
The method enables automatic interpretation of latent directions without manual inspection.
It supports a broader range of analysis compared to previous methods limited by manual interpretation or few trained vectors.
papers.limitation: Variability due to random seed initialization affects the sampled h-space vectors.
future_direction: Reducing the effect of random seed initialization on sampled results
Extending analysis with quantifiable metrics on broader domains
papers.abstract: Recent advances in image generation have made diffusion models powerful tools for creating high-quality images. However, their iterative denoising process makes understanding and interpreting their semantic latent spaces more challenging than other generative models, such as GANs. Recent methods have attempted to address this issue by identifying semantically meaningful directions within the latent space. However, they often need manual interpretation or are limited in the number of vectors that can be trained, restricting their scope and utility. This paper proposes a novel framework for unsupervised exploration of diffusion latent spaces. We directly leverage natural language prompts and image captions to map latent directions. This method allows for the automatic understanding of hidden features and supports a broader range of analysis without the need to train specific vectors. Our method provides a more scalable and interpretable understanding of the semantic knowledge encoded within diffusion models, facilitating comprehensive analysis of latent biases and the nuanced representations these models learn. Experimental results show that our framework can uncover hidden patterns and associations in various domains, offering new insights into the interpretability of diffusion model latent spaces.

papers.title: Attribution Patching Outperforms Automated Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: Does a simple method based on attribution patching outperform existing automated circuit discovery methods in identifying circuits?
papers.core_contribution: Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) outperforms existing automated circuit discovery methods like ACDC in identifying circuits while being substantially faster, requiring only two forward passes and one backward pass.
papers.conclusion: Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) outperforms ACDC in identifying circuits and is faster, but its results can be improved by running ACDC on the pruned subgraph found by EAP.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) has greater AUC for circuit recovery than ACDC on the IOI and Greater-Than tasks.
EAP is more efficient than activation patching, requiring only two forward passes and a backward pass.
The linear approximation of activation patching by attribution patching is not always accurate, especially when the task-specific metric is concave.
Running ACDC on the pruned subgraph returned by EAP can improve the identification of relevant edges.
Attribution scores for edges in the ground-truth circuit tend to be spread further from zero than edges not in the circuit.
papers.limitation:
The linear approximation used by attribution patching can be inaccurate, especially for edges from the model's embeddings, leading to overestimation of edge importance.
The metrics used for interpretability (e.g., circuit recovery against human-found circuits) do not precisely capture meaningful human understanding and are limited by the imperfections of human-found circuits.
future_direction: Future circuit discovery experiments should run EAP first and then apply ACDC on the pruned subgraph.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: Interpreting Large Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse dictionary learning methods (Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations) be scaled and applied to interpret and control large text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: This work successfully scales Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) to a large text-to-image diffusion model (FLUX.1), demonstrating they can decompose residual stream activations into interpretable features and enable targeted steering of image generation.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations are effective methods for interpreting and steering large text-to-image diffusion models, with SAE features being particularly suitable for manipulating concrete semantic concepts in generated images.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and outperform MLP neurons on automated interpretability metrics.
ITDA achieves comparable interpretability to SAEs but tends to encode more abstract visual attributes (colors, textures) while SAE features capture more concrete objects.
Steering image generation via SAE feature activation addition is effective but constrained, requiring the initial prompt to be semantically related to the steered feature.
The residual stream activations in FLUX.1 are highly anisotropic, necessitating PCA whitening for effective SAE training to avoid a high proportion of dead features.
ITDA generally achieves superior reconstruction performance compared to SAEs at similar dictionary sizes.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability (autointerp) metrics do not distinguish between abstract visual properties and manipulable semantic concepts, a qualitative difference observed between ITDA and SAE features.
Steering with SAE features is constrained and only effective when the initial image prompt is semantically related to the feature being added.
The autointerp pipeline may have biases, such as picking up on simple image characteristics like color rather than the intended semantic feature.
future_direction: Applying SAEs to vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation (sparse probing).
Adapting the SAE encoder architecture to incorporate spatial inductive bias (e.g., convolutional layers) for image data.
Improving steering techniques, potentially by making the process more similar to finetuning or otherwise more aware of steering effects.
Investigating shared features between the text and image streams of the multimodal DiT architecture.
Comparing the two FLUX.1 variants (Dev and Schnell) using methods like crosscoders to find corresponding or unique features.
Investigating biases specific to the automated interpretability pipeline.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders are a promising new approach for decomposing language model activations for interpretation and control. They have been applied successfully to vision transformer image encoders and to small-scale diffusion models. Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) is a recently proposed variant of dictionary learning that takes the dictionary to be a set of data points from the activation distribution and reconstructs them with gradient pursuit. We apply Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and ITDA to a large text-to-image diffusion model, Flux 1, and consider the interpretability of embeddings of both by introducing a visual automated interpretation pipeline. We find that SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and beat MLP neurons on interpretability. We are able to use SAE features to steer image generation through activation addition. We find that ITDA has comparable interpretability to SAEs.

papers.title: Understanding the Latent Space of Diffusion Models through the Lens of Riemannian Geometry
papers.research_question: How can we understand the latent space of diffusion models from a geometrical perspective, and how does this structure evolve during the generative process and with text conditions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a geometric analysis of the latent space of diffusion models using the pullback metric, enabling unsupervised image editing via latent basis traversal and providing insights into how the latent structure evolves during generation and with text conditions.
papers.conclusion: The geometric analysis of diffusion models' latent space using the pullback metric provides a deeper understanding and opens new possibilities for adopting diffusion models in useful applications.
papers.key_findings:
The discovered local latent basis enables semantic image editing by moving the latent variable xt along the basis vector at a specific timestep.
The geometric structure of the latent space evolves from low-frequency to high-frequency components during the generative process, confirming coarse-to-fine generation.
The discrepancy between tangent spaces of different samples increases along the generative process, making generally applicable editing directions harder to find later.
Diffusion models trained on simpler datasets (e.g., CelebA-HQ) exhibit more consistent tangent spaces across timesteps compared to complex datasets (e.g., ImageNet).
Similar text prompts yield similar tangent spaces, and the influence of the prompt on the tangent space becomes weaker in later timesteps.
papers.limitation:
Entanglement of semantic directions due to dataset biases (e.g., beard editing converting female to male).
Occasional abrupt changes during editing in Stable Diffusion, highlighting the complex geometry of the latent space.
The method assumes the feature space H has a Euclidean metric, which may not hold for other architectural designs.
future_direction: Exploring the reasons behind the effectiveness of x-space guidance.
Investigating the disentanglement capability of the latent space X compared to the feature space H.
Analyzing the latent space of other architectural designs, such as transformer-based diffusion models.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of diffusion models (DMs), we still lack a thorough understanding of their latent space. To understand the latent space $\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathcal{X}$, we analyze them from a geometrical perspective. Our approach involves deriving the local latent basis within $\mathcal{X}$ by leveraging the pullback metric associated with their encoding feature maps. Remarkably, our discovered local latent basis enables image editing capabilities by moving $\mathbf{x}_t$, the latent space of DMs, along the basis vector at specific timesteps. We further analyze how the geometric structure of DMs evolves over diffusion timesteps and differs across different text conditions. This confirms the known phenomenon of coarse-to-fine generation, as well as reveals novel insights such as the discrepancy between $\mathbf{x}_t$ across timesteps, the effect of dataset complexity, and the time-varying influence of text prompts. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to present image editing through $\mathbf{x}$-space traversal, editing only once at specific timestep $t$ without any additional training, and providing thorough analyses of the latent structure of DMs. The code to reproduce our experiments can be found at https://github.com/enkeejunior1/Diffusion-Pullback.

papers.title: Query Circuits: Explaining How Language Models Answer User Prompts
papers.research_question: How can we explain why a language model produces a particular output for a specific input query by tracing the information flow inside the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces query circuit discovery for local, input-level explanations of LLMs, proposes a robust evaluation metric (NDF) and sampling-based methods (BoN) to efficiently identify sparse, faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: Query circuit discovery, aided by BoN sampling and NDF, demonstrates that compact sub-networks can explain much of an LLM's behavior on individual queries, offering a promising path for scalable, faithful explanations of LLM decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Extremely sparse query circuits (e.g., 1.3% of edges) can recover a large portion (e.g., 60%) of model performance on individual queries.
Best-of-N (BoN) sampling effectively discovers faithful query circuits, outperforming baseline methods.
Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF) is a more robust evaluation metric for query circuits compared to Normalized Faithfulness Score (NFS).
Query circuits enable local, prompt-level explanations of LLM decisions, offering a step towards scalable interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The method neglects combinatorial interactions among edges, which is a fundamental limitation of using indirect effects as edge scores.
The work focuses on queries with single-token outputs (e.g., option IDs) and does not address multi-token generations.
There is no automated method for interpreting the functionalities of identified edges and nodes; manual investigation is not scalable.
future_direction: Develop methods to account for combinatorial interactions among edges in circuit discovery.
Extend query circuit discovery to multi-token generations.
Integrate automated interpretability methods to explain the functionalities of discovered circuits.
papers.abstract: Explaining why a language model produces a particular output requires local, input-level explanations. Existing methods uncover global capability circuits (e.g., indirect object identification), but not why the model answers a specific input query in a particular way. We introduce query circuits, which directly trace the information flow inside a model that maps a specific input to the output. Unlike surrogate-based approaches (e.g., sparse autoencoders), query circuits are identified within the model itself, resulting in more faithful and computationally accessible explanations. To make query circuits practical, we address two challenges. First, we introduce Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF), a robust metric to evaluate how well a discovered circuit recovers the model's decision for a specific input, and is broadly applicable to circuit discovery beyond our setting. Second, we develop sampling-based methods to efficiently identify circuits that are sparse yet faithfully describe the model's behavior. Across benchmarks (IOI, arithmetic, MMLU, and ARC), we find that there exist extremely sparse query circuits within the model that can recover much of its performance on single queries. For example, a circuit covering only 1.3% of model connections can recover about 60% of performance on an MMLU questions. Overall, query circuits provide a step towards faithful, scalable explanations of how language models process individual inputs.

papers.title: Exploiting Interpretable Capabilities with Concept-Enhanced Diffusion and Prototype Networks
papers.research_question: How can concept information be leveraged to increase interpretability in machine learning models by integrating it into existing architectures to obtain visual concept representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces concept-enhanced methods that incorporate concept information into existing architectures to generate visual concept representations and perform interpretable concept prediction.
papers.conclusion: Concept-enhanced methods successfully incorporate concept information into existing architectures, enabling the generation of concept-based samples or prototypes and interpretable concept prediction without significant performance loss compared to black-box methods.
papers.key_findings:
Concept-Guided Conditional Diffusion can generate images conditioned on both positive and negative concepts, successfully visualizing concept information.
Concept-Guided Prototype Networks can accurately predict binary concepts and generate interpretable prototype patches for each concept class.
The proposed methods achieve concept prediction accuracy close to a black-box oracle while providing interpretability through visual concept representations.
The methods work on real-world datasets (CUB and AwA2) and with various base architectures (DenseNets, ResNets, VGGs).
The expressivity of concepts is exploited, allowing for generations where direct human interpretation is not trivial (e.g., negative concept guidance).
papers.limitation:
The method relies on concept-annotated datasets.
Generating images with diffusion models is computationally expensive.
future_direction: Extend the work to the continuous concept domain.
Use concept-enhanced methods to understand and mitigate data leakage in Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs).
Use less computationally demanding variations of diffusion models (e.g., latent diffusion).
papers.abstract: Concept-based machine learning methods have increasingly gained importance due to the growing interest in making neural networks interpretable. However, concept annotations are generally challenging to obtain, making it crucial to leverage all their prior knowledge. By creating concept-enriched models that incorporate concept information into existing architectures, we exploit their interpretable capabilities to the fullest extent. In particular, we propose Concept-Guided Conditional Diffusion, which can generate visual representations of concepts, and Concept-Guided Prototype Networks, which can create a concept prototype dataset and leverage it to perform interpretable concept prediction. These results open up new lines of research by exploiting pre-existing information in the quest for rendering machine learning more human-understandable.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Diffusion Models Generate Images Like Painters: an Analytical Theory of Outline First, Details Later
papers.research_question: How do diffusion generative models convert pure noise into meaningful images? The paper investigates whether diffusion models generate images by first committing to an outline and then adding details, and provides a theoretical explanation for this behavior.
papers.core_contribution: The paper derives a closed-form solution to the probability flow ODE for a Gaussian distribution, which explains the 'outline-first, details-later' behavior in diffusion models and can be used to accelerate sampling by skipping early steps.
papers.conclusion: Diffusion models generate images by first committing to an outline and then adding finer details, similar to how painters work. The theoretical analysis provides a geometric understanding of the diffusion process and links it to image retrieval.
papers.key_findings:
Reverse diffusion trajectories are effectively two-dimensional and resemble rotations within the plane defined by the initial noise and final image.
High-variance scene features (e.g., layout) emerge earlier in the generation process than low-variance details.
Early perturbations during reverse diffusion have a greater impact on image content than later perturbations.
The Gaussian solution accurately predicts the early phase of reverse diffusion for pre-trained models.
A hybrid sampling method that uses the Gaussian solution to skip early steps can accelerate generation without degrading image quality.
papers.limitation:
The Gaussian approximation is only accurate early in reverse diffusion and breaks down later when the distribution becomes multi-modal.
For larger images, the Gaussian approximation is less effective due to difficulties in estimating the covariance matrix from limited data.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other diffusion formulations such as Poisson flow generative models.
Combine the acceleration method with other advanced samplers.
papers.abstract: How do diffusion generative models convert pure noise into meaningful images? In a variety of pretrained diffusion models (including conditional latent space models like Stable Diffusion), we observe that the reverse diffusion process that underlies image generation has the following properties: (i) individual trajectories tend to be low-dimensional and resemble 2D `rotations'; (ii) high-variance scene features like layout tend to emerge earlier, while low-variance details tend to emerge later; and (iii) early perturbations tend to have a greater impact on image content than later perturbations. To understand these phenomena, we derive and study a closed-form solution to the probability flow ODE for a Gaussian distribution, which shows that the reverse diffusion state rotates towards a gradually-specified target on the image manifold. It also shows that generation involves first committing to an outline, and then to finer and finer details. We find that this solution accurately describes the initial phase of image generation for pretrained models, and can in principle be used to make image generation more efficient by skipping reverse diffusion steps. Finally, we use our solution to characterize the image manifold in Stable Diffusion. Our viewpoint reveals an unexpected similarity between generation by GANs and diffusion and provides a conceptual link between diffusion and image retrieval.

papers.title: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Under what conditions does a transparent algorithm constitute a faithful interpretation of the known, but opaque, low-level details of a black box model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper generalizes the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement to arbitrary mechanism transformation, and uses this framework to provide a flexible, precise formalization for core mechanistic interpretability concepts (polysemantic neurons, linear representation hypothesis, modular features, graded faithfulness) and to unify a wide range of existing interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Causal abstraction provides a solid theoretical foundation for mechanistic interpretability, enabling precise definitions of core concepts and a unified perspective on existing methods, which facilitates rigorous falsification through experimentation.
papers.key_findings:
Causal abstraction theory is generalized to allow for arbitrary mechanism transformations (interventionals), which enables the isolation of quantities distributed across overlapping sets of microvariables.
The core concepts of polysemantic neurons, the linear representation hypothesis, modular features, and graded faithfulness are given flexible, mathematically precise definitions within the causal abstraction framework.
A wide range of mechanistic interpretability methods (e.g., activation patching, causal scrubbing, sparse autoencoders, steering) and behavioral interpretability methods (e.g., LIME, integrated gradients) are unified under the common language of causal abstraction.
papers.abstract: Causal abstraction provides a theoretical foundation for mechanistic interpretability, the field concerned with providing intelligible algorithms that are faithful simplifications of the known, but opaque low-level details of black box AI models. Our contributions are (1) generalizing the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement (i.e., hard and soft interventions) to arbitrary mechanism transformation (i.e., functionals from old mechanisms to new mechanisms), (2) providing a flexible, yet precise formalization for the core concepts of polysemantic neurons, the linear representation hypothesis, modular features, and graded faithfulness, and (3) unifying a variety of mechanistic interpretability methods in the common language of causal abstraction, namely, activation and path patching, causal mediation analysis, causal scrubbing, causal tracing, circuit analysis, concept erasure, sparse autoencoders, differential binary masking, distributed alignment search, and steering.

papers.title: Decompose the model: Mechanistic interpretability in image models with Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG)
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be achieved in image models by systematically tracing the pathway from input to output across an entire dataset, moving beyond class-specific explanations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel approach for mechanistic interpretability in image models, using Pointwise Feature Vectors (PFVs) and Effective Receptive Fields (ERFs) to decompose model embeddings into interpretable Concept Vectors, and a new Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG) method to trace their causal contributions across layers for a dataset-wide analysis.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a novel approach for extracting and attributing concepts within image models, enabling a comprehensive layer-wise analysis that advances mechanistic interpretability by moving from class-specific to dataset-wide explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The method can extract and attribute 'shared concepts' that are common across similar classes, unlike class-specific explanation methods.
The proposed concept extraction method using bisecting k-means clustering outperforms other methods (like Sparse AutoEncoder and dictionary learning) in fidelity metrics (C-Deletion and C-Insertion) across most layers.
The Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG) method effectively quantifies the causal relationships between concept vectors across different layers, validated by inter-layer deletion/insertion experiments.
